#732. EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game

John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29 FA Cup finals for BBC Sport

Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.

Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.

It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.

With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.

The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.

Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.

"I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (Â£42bn) in August, told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.

The BBC's lead football commentator Guy Mowbray said it was a "privilege" to be involved in the game, which he has provided commentary for since 2023.

"I think it's quite a nice, sort of non-scary use of AI," he said.

"We're in the business of nostalgia... I hear commentary not in my own voice, but in John's voice, because that's the voice I knew growing up.

"So I think it's nice that that legacy can be continued in this way."

WATCH: The new John Motson commentary in EA Sports FC 27 - and how it sounded back in Fifa 1998

John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.

"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.

EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.

"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.

Gazza's tears, Radford's screamer & the Crazy Gang - 5 of Motty's best

Motson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.

"My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.

"So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects."

But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.

"If someone has signed a deal allowing their likeness to be used after they die, I have no issue with that," he said.

"But in life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed.

"Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either."

One of the main arguments against the use of generative AI in video games is that it can replace humans - something that EA was keen to argue against.

"From a gaming standpoint, it's something we've used for many years - like machine learning to help drive animation systems and so on and so forth," Prior said.

"It's not there to replace commentators in any way shape or form... there's certainly no future plans to replace anyone with AI."

Derek Rae, who has been a commentator in EA FC for several years, said the tech could make things easier, but he still spent a long time recording dialogue in studios.

"It's quite a lot of days in the course of a year," he said. "So it might be two or three times a month that we do it in season for the game, which is typically sort of November time through until May.

"The more creative things have to be done with the human voice because they have to have the personality, sometimes a little chuckle thrown in the middle of a sentence or a little idiosyncrasy," he said.

"But when it comes to the more normal features in a video game, for example, routine surnames like Smith and Jones and Brown, that's something that AI can probably accomplish quite easily."

Josko Gvardiol tackling Jamal Musiala in FC 27 - perhaps examples of some less routine surnames

Rae said he was excited about the Motson project - but wasn't convinced he would follow suit.

"If we're being modest, we might say, well, no, I don't want to inflict my voice on the next generation."

He told BBC News it was something he would need to "think about" it but added: "I'm hopefully many years away from having to make a decision like that."

#731. AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

Research suggests that students who aren't careful about how they use ChatGPT and other AI tools risk poorer academic outcomes. It's a huge challenge for teachers.

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#730. 'Justice for sport' - Afcon reaction as Senegal reinstated as winners

Senegal's football federation reacted to the Cas verdict on social media with a picture of the side lifting the Afcon trophy alongside the caption "again and always champions of Africa"

That was the initial reaction of Senegal football federation (FSF) president Abdoulaye Fall to the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to reinstate the West Africans as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions.

The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 in January's final but were stripped of the title in March by a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board, which imposed a 3-0 forfeit after they walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty awarded against them when the game was goalless.

Following a hearing in Lausanne in October, a three-man Cas panel unanimously overturned that ruling by Caf, effectively judging that the decisions taken by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala in restarting the match and playing it to a conclusion were final.

Morocco's football federation (FRMF), however, says it will "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".

The North Africans could yet take their fight to the Swiss Federal Court.

Those in Senegal have celebrated the return of the title, while several legal experts have backed the Cas verdict.

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling

Senegal's talisman Sadio Mane, who was named player of the tournament at Afcon 2025, said the ruling "fills us with joy".

The 34-year-old former Liverpool man thanked his team-mates and Senegal staff as well as the whole Senegalese nation at home and abroad.

"Your faith in us gave us strength during the most difficult moments. This victory is yours, too," he said in a statement on social media.

Senegal captain Kalidou Koulibaly, who missed the final through injury, echoed that sentiment.

"Some victories are won on the pitch, while others are won in the heart of a people," he said in a post on Facebook.

"Long before this verdict, there was you - your prayers, your flags in the windows, your fervour, and the pride that unites us all: the pride of the people of Teranga."

Pape Gueye, the man who scored the extra-time winner in Rabat, described the Cas decision as "an immense relief".

Both he and Mane had a message of support for Morocco.

"Senegal and Morocco are brotherly nations; may our shared passion for football continue to bring us closer together," Mane said.

Gueye added: "Beyond football, the respect and fraternity between our two peoples remain what matters most. Let's hold on to that.

Afcon: Is the Senegal v Morocco saga finally over?

Morocco's main complaint is that Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon tournament regulations - which were implemented by the Caf appeals board in March - were not followed by Cas.

Article 82 states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".

Article 84 then states a 3-0 forfeit should be imposed on a team which is eliminated in such circumstances.

"There [are] football rules that should have been applied by the referee," former Morocco international Hassan Kachloul told BBC Sport.

"When the Senegalese players left the pitch, the game should have been over."

The FRMF registered its "surprise" at the Cas decision and said that the panel "failed to account for the stance recently established" by the International Football Association Board (Ifab), the game's ultimate lawmakers, and world governing body Fifa regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee's permission.

However, Ifab only updated its laws in April - three months after the Afcon final - to state that a referee may send off any player who leaves the field when protesting a decision.

Moroccan football journalist Jalal Bounouar says his compatriots are "frustrated and disappointed" by the ruling.

"The main reason is that Caf's appeal board had already applied Article 82 and 84 of the competition regulations which considered Senegal to have forfeited the match," he told Newsday on the BBC World Service.

"Many Moroccans feel the decision by Cas has ignored the importance of these rules. From the Moroccan perspective, the referee should have taken stronger disciplinary action.

"We feel that our team was put in a difficult situation and that the final was not managed fairly."

Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 champions - ten months on

Cas has a long-standing practice of following what has been called the 'field of play' doctrine.

It refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".

"The primary argument was that the referee is the master of the decision on the pitch," said Serge Vittoz, a member of the FSF's legal team.

Raymond Hack, both a former head of disciplinary at Caf and a former arbiter at Cas, said the judgement was the "correct verdict".

"What everyone seems to forget - and whilst there may be contradictory information in Article 82 and 84 - decisions taken by the referee during the match are final," the South African told the BBC World Service.

"Only the referee can start a game. Only a referee can end a game."

For former Nigeria striker Daniel Amokachi, an Afcon winner in 1994, the Cas ruling is "the right decision".

"At the end of the day, the man in charge of the match (Ndala) restarted the game, the game ended," he said.

Caf president Patrice Motsepe has repeatedly said his organisation will respect and adhere to Cas' decision

Caf has already tightened its own regulations to avoid a repeat.

But Algerian sports journalist Maher Mezahi says the continental governing body still needs to salvage its image.

"How many times have we seen Caf's legal institutions, whether it be the disciplinary board or the appeals committee, come up with these decisions that we all find ridiculous," he said.

"They end up being challenged at Cas and eventually they get overturned.

"We have to rebuild trust in Caf's own judicial bodies because it is a little bit humiliating and degrading and it brings the entire reputation of the confederation into disrepute."

The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to take place in June and July next year, and Senegal and Morocco were among the first qualifiers earlier this month.

Kachloul says the next tournament provides a chance to draw a definitive line under what happened in Rabat in January.

"This event, wherever you look at it on the Senegalese side or Moroccan side, doesn't look good at all," the one-time Aston Villa midfielder said.

"They are lucky to have another [Afcon] tournament in six months to redeem themselves and to paint a better picture of African football.

"The best way to prove that you're the best is to go back on the pitch and let the football talk."

#729. SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.

That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.

Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.

"In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit.

He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.)

Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.)

The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.

Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions, and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.

So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk.

"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.

And SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the company wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.

This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites, and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that.

Assembly of that new Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #728. Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?

Manchester United are in the Premier League relegation zone 11 games into the season

Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.

Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?

While Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points last term, they actually started the season better than United have this season. After 11 games in 2025-26, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.

But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

While the table prompted talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.

United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.

But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.

While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.

Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

And it is not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.

By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the percentage chance of each club finishing in each position.

While the above means it is more likely United will survive, it is worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

There is a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.

History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.

Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.

A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.

Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.

Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there would not be entirely unprecedented.

It is a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they have played than they did last season.

Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last term.

Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.

While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals.

So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his new club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

#726. A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains. Credit: 3DMedisphere/SPL

In the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

Although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

Scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

“We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” says Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in New York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”

This year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very important milestone,” says Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

Success is by no means guaranteed, says Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” says Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

The latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” says Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City.

Starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” says Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

One overarching problem, says Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

That attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” says Burton.

Researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, says Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

To mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

Source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Sanders says that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, says virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants

In small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” says Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

#725. Will Smith Makes Surprise Cameo for Tatyana Ali in DWTS Finale

Will Smith supported his Fresh Prince of Bel-Air costar Tatyana Ali during the Dancing With the Stars finale with a sweet message of support before winners were crowned.

Now this is a story all about how Will Smith and Tatyana Ali melted hearts during the Dancing With the Stars finale.

Before Ezra Frech and professional partner Daniella Karagach were crowned the winners of DWTS season 35, the Fresh Prince of Bel-Air actor showed face to support his former costar.

“I am amazed,” Smith said in a video package that aired just before winners were announced during the Nov. 24 episode. “I am in awe. I am inspired. Keep doing what you’re doing. I love you.”

While Ali was floored by the support she received—which also included Elmo and The Black Eyed Peas’ will.i.am—she was visibly shocked by Smith’s brief cameo, falling to the ground and putting her hand over her mouth as she stood by her professional dance partner Jan Ravnik.

“I was surprised by all of them,” Ali later told ABC News after the finale. “I didn’t know about Will, I didn’t know about Elmo.”

Although she and Ravnik didn’t come out with a Mirrorball trophy, Ali insisted she had a “magical” experience competing on the series.

“From the first performance all the way to this one,” she mused. “Tonight was amazing. Tonight was really miraculous.”

Smith’s appearance may have briefly turned DWTS into a Fresh Prince of Bel-Air reunion—Alfonso Ribiero, who played Carlton Banks, has been hosting the reality series since 2022—but it was far from the only must-see moment of the night.

Case in point: Frech seamlessly recovered during his final performance to Linkin Park’s “Numb” alongside Karagach after a malfunction with his leg prosthetic. As Frech seamlessly reattached the piece mid-performance, Ribiero shared his awe in a commentary, noting, “What an incredible recovery.”

Naturally, Frech earned plenty of praise from the judges following his final performance.

“Ezra, you are a hero,” Derek Hough said in his feedback. “This performance will have a ripple effect far beyond this show. What you did tonight—forever, kids will look up to you and see what’s possible. The fact that the worst-case scenario might have happened and you wouldn’t have even known.”

#724. Leicester no longer for sale as owner looks to future

King Power, the Thai business that Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha is part of, bought Leicester for Â£35m in 2010

Leicester City owner Khun Aiyawatt 'Top' Srivaddhanaprabha has confirmed the one-time Premier League title winners are no longer up for sale and there will be a "refocus" on rebuilding the side after years of decline.

The Foxes were put on the market in the summer after back-to-back relegations saw the side drop from the Premier League and straight through the Championship to land in England's third tier for just the second time in the club's 142-year history.

A sales brochure was produced by US investment bank Citigroup in which an asking price of more than Â£200m was put on a League One club that a decade ago had defied all expectations by winning the Premier League title at 5,000-1 odds.

Leicester never publicly acknowledged that the club had been put up for sale, with under-fire chief football officer Jon Rudkin going so far as to say he "cannot comment on speculation" when asked about it in a rare interview with BBC Radio Leicester in October.

Khun Top, however, has now said that there were no takers when investment had been sought for a side that the Srivaddhanaprabha family, through its King Power duty free business in Thailand, have owned for 16 years.

"We recently undertook a structured process to explore whether new investment or a change of ownership could actually be the right thing for the club," Khun Top wrote in an open letter to Leicester City supporters on the club's website., external

"Those discussions have not resulted in an agreement, and I have decided to conclude the process to enable us to refocus on the work needed to move the club forward."

'Business as always' - Foxes boss Martin brushes off sales talk

Listen to BBC Radio Leicester's When You're Smiling podcast

Pre-match, post-match and topical Foxes content

Three relegations in four years, having yo-yoed between the Premier League and Championship before going down to League One, has badly damaged the relationship between the Foxes' owners and their supporter base.

While a golden age of success was bankrolled by King Power, with Premier League glory in 2016 followed up by FA Cup success in 2021, high spending on an underperforming side in recent years has led to an increasing number of supporters calling for Khun Top to sell up.

But the Thai businessman said he has a "deep connection" to Leicester and "its people".

And it is not just euphoric sporting moments that have forged the bond he is talking about, as his father - and predecessor as Foxes chairman - Khun Vichai died in a helicopter crash outside the stadium in 2018.

"For my family and me, Leicester City has been a big part of our lives for many years," he said.

"We have experienced extraordinary moments together, as well as some very difficult ones."

Khun Top added that the struggles of recent years, which included the club being hit with a points penalty last season for breaking spending rules, has got him "thinking a lot about our direction".

Earlier this year he told BBC Radio Leicester that he shoulders the blame for the club's decline.

"Making better decisions" as well as "continuing to learn from our past experiences" are two steps the club "need to take", he said.

Khun Top has insisted that through King Power, a company that has endured difficulties in recent years, the club's "financial position remains secure".

However, he added that there was "work needed to put Leicester City on a more sustainable footing".

"That has been a principle behind the work and decisions of the last year â giving the club the appropriate support for its immediate circumstances, while building the organisational discipline and financial resilience that will underpin a responsible plan for future growth," he said.

As part of Khun Top's missive, he confirmed that chief executive Kevin Davies will be stepping down from the role in December.

Davies had only been in the job since March, and was promoted to the position after a shake-up of a number of leadership roles.

#723. Can a 'coalition of the willing' create momentum for a fossil fuel phaseout?

In April, about 60 countries held an unprecedented meeting in Colombia to work out a plan to slowly quit oil, coal and gas. How influential is this coalition at the COP31 climate summit?

This time last year, as negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Brazil entered crunch time, there was hope that governments would agree on a clear roadmap for phasing out oil, gas and coal. More than 80 countries backed the idea.

But instead, after opposition from oil-producing states such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, the conference wrapped up with a watered-down final agreement that did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.

As a compromise, summit host Brazil offered to produce a "voluntary" roadmap. At the same time, a group of 57 countries frustrated with the deadlock at the consensus-based UN talks decided to form a "coalition of the willing" to accelerate the fossil fuel exit outside the COP framework.

They held their own summit in April in Santa Marta, Colombia — the first such conference to specifically focus on implementing the transition away from fossil fuels (referred to as TAFF).

Co-hosted by Colombia and the Netherlands, the Santa Marta conference brought together countries including Canada, Norway, Brazil, Nigeria, Mexico, Australia and Germany, as well as highly climate-vulnerable states such as Vanuatu.

The idea was for governments to start developing national roadmaps and working out how to restructure their financial and trade systems to wean themselves off polluting energy sources — an incredibly complicated undertaking, particularly for developing countries dependent on revenue from fossil fuel exports.

Part of their discussions focused on cutting subsidies for oil, coal and gas, as well as supporting people whose livelihoods rely on the fossil fuel industry to find new forms of income.

A little over six months on from the Santa Marta meeting, representatives from almost 200 countries are holding talks in Antalya, Turkey, as part of the latest UN climate conference.

Countries agreed for the first time in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels — the main driver behind rising global temperatures. But summits since then have failed to pin down how to implement that pledge.

It's not yet clear whether the Santa Marta coalition will influence ambition at this year's COP.

"I think it's more of a long-term game," said Chetna Hareesh Kumar, a climate policy analyst at the Berlin-based research organization NewClimate Institute.

She says it's too soon to expect the coalition to have an influence on the negotiations but adds that that could change at future COPs. The grouping could bring more nations on board if, for example, it shows it can be truly inclusive, address the needs of different types of countries and show that a transition is feasible.

One role the group is playing, according to Alexandra Scott, a senior climate diplomacy adviser at Italian climate change think tank ECCO, is "keeping up the political momentum," and showing "that there is this huge group of countries who really want to accelerate this transition away from fossil fuels."

She says it's also building an invaluable "cadre of knowledge" on how to develop national TAFF plans and deal with barriers individual countries face — like how to secure funding for the infrastructure investments needed for the energy transition.

The Santa Marta group is "really answering a lot of the questions that countries have always had on how on earth do we even start to transition our whole economy off fossil fuels?" Scott said.

This expertise being shared and tested in practice can show what such a transformation could look like and the knowledge brought into COP, added Scott.

Since the Santa Marta conference, Germany, France and the Netherlands have released national plans to phase out fossil fuels. While the plans contain no new commitments, experts see them as a positive first step.

Kumar says more countries could announce similar plans just ahead of the second TAFF summit in Tuvalu next year. Finland presented its TAFF roadmap in the first week of COP, but analysts do not expect many more countries to follow suit soon.

Another potential boost that could get momentum going is Brazil's recently published global roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, promised at last year's COP.

The nearly 200-page document seeks to serve as a toolkit for countries shifting from fossil fuels to renewable energy, such as wind and solar. It envisages countries making a phased transition between 2028 and 2033.

The aim, Ana Toni, CEO of last year's COP, told AP, is to break down the transition into "smaller actionable solutions" and help countries make practical progress.

The roadmap suggests measures tailored to each country's circumstances, including dependence on fossil fuel and financial capacities. "Levers" it proposes include reducing fossil fuel subsidies, expanding renewable energy and cutting methane emissions.

Kumar called it a "customizable" approach that allows every country to take action, regardless of its situation. "The question really is now what countries do with it and how much momentum they can generate," she added.

This year's climate change summit in Turkey — taking place after a series of deadly heat waves in Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people — isn't expected to result in any big announcements about fossil fuels.

Global renewable energy capacity has surged in recent years, making up a third of the world's power generation for the first time in 2025. But many countries still rely on coal, oil and gas.

A database compiled by the German environmental organization Urgewald shows that most oil and gas companies worldwide, among them QatarEnergy, Saudi Aramco and Russia's Gazprom, are exploring or developing new reserves.

Meanwhile, subsidies for fossil fuels amount to around $920 billion (around €830 billion) per year, according to data from the OECD, but that number is falling.

One issue Turkey is pushing at the COP conference is electrification. It's calling on countries to endorse the goal of 35% of final energy consumption coming from electricity by 2035 — up from around 20% today.

The pledge has drawn criticism from some circles, though, for leaving open whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources.

Ideally, Kumar said, electrification would be powered by renewables and tied to a goal of phasing out polluting fossil fuels.

"If something like that could make it to the final text, that would be a really good sign for momentum."

Assimilate this! How cyber-zombies and the "birth of 'Star Trek'" gave Jean-Luc Picard one of his finest hours.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.

With the Borg overrunning the newly launched USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch.

But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive.

It's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect.

And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath.

In 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after "The Next Generation" ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the big-screen frontier alone.

William Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors.

While "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These plans were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights.

They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063, the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship.

"We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross.

"The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me."

Paramount reportedly flirted with big-name directors like Ridley Scott ("Alien", "Blade Runner") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more important than big-screen experience.

The film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle.

The Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done".

They arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name.

But as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew.

Initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his new-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest.

These Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and new extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and "Aliens" as inspiration.

"[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg."

The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen Borg Queen (brilliantly played by Alice Krige) to act as spokesperson for the Collective.

Bringing a singular entity to a civilisation built on the notion that there's no "I" in "team" was a controversial move, but it made perfect dramatic sense. Indeed, a legion of drones would have little chance of seducing Data, even if it was just for 0.68 seconds.

"We wrestled with it quite a bit before we committed to [the Borg Queen's] character," Moore told Syfy Wire, "because it was a choice that was also antithetical to the idea of the Borg. The whole concept of these villains was that they were a collection, and that there were no individuals. And that's what made them the faceless, implacable 'resistance is futile' enemy. But it also limited how to deal with them dramatically because it meant that any scenes you always had to deal with this sort of collective voice. We decided that the story would be better if we had some individual to deal with."

The Queen was also granted one of the greatest entrances in sci-fi history, as her head and torso were lowered into a robot body with a bit of help from Industrial Light & Magic.

The Starfleet armada's assault on the Borg was similarly impressive and effectively a test run for "The Phantom Menace", as ILM's visual effects supervisor John Knoll pioneered the CG effects pipeline that would later become pivotal to the "Star Wars" prequels. It was also a brilliant excuse to introduce several new starship designs to the "Trek" canon.

They're standout moments in a film that made the most of its comparatively puny budget of $45 million (reported). (For comparison, "Independence Day", which was released the same year — and also featured Brent Spiner — cost closer to $75 million.)

As Moore later recalled in an interview with the Hollywood Reporter, "Paramount had their formula. They said that 'Star Trek' movies only make this amount of money. So, therefore, you can only have this amount of budget to make it. And, at that point, we were still — just like on the TV show — counting phaser beam effects shots [to keep the price down]."

The studio needn't have worried. "First Contact" was a huge hit with fans and became one of the franchise's highest-grossing films at the box office. Borg mythology introduced here (including the Queen) would become a mainstay on "Star Trek: Voyager", while Jean-Luc would get to face his cybernetic white whale again in "Picard" — though the incomparable Stewart arguably never again had another "Trek" scene to rival the ones he had here.

"Fortunately it happened to be a wonderful script, and my job was not to screw it up," said Frakes. "It also holds up as a movie that just happens to be a 'Star Trek' movie, which we were all hoping would be the case."

'Star Trek: First Contact' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

Watch Star Trek: First Contact on Paramount+:Essential (ads): $8.99/mo or $89.99/yrPremium (no ads): $13.99/mo or $139.99/yr

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

#721. Watford appoint Iordanescu as head coach

Edward Iordanescu took Romania to the last 16 at Euro 2024

Watford have appointed former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu as the Championship club's new head coach.

The 48-year-old replaces Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge following a run of seven defeats in their past 10 league games, culminating in Saturday's 4-0 loss to Sheffield United.

"I am very proud and happy to be at this football club," Iordanescu told the club website., external

"I can see the team is in a difficult moment but I have already watched many of the games over the last few days and I'm very confident about the future."

He becomes Watford's sixth new boss in less than 18 months and is the 25th manager since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

Pioneer or coach-eater? The complex world of Pozzo's Watford

The former CFR Cluj and Legia Warsaw manager will be joined at Watford by backroom staff Alexandru Radu, Grzegorz Mokry and Michele Iannucci, but will watch Wednesday's Championship match at home to Blackburn Rovers from the stands before taking charge for Saturday's game at Derby.

Adrian Mariappa will oversee Wednesday's match at Vicarage Road (19:45 GMT), alongside Paul Furlong and Lloyd Doyley.

The Watford job is Iordanescu's first since leaving Legia Warsaw in October 2025, where he won the Super Cup last season.

It is the 10th managerial post of his 15-year coaching career, which has taken in Bulgarian club CSKA Sofia as well as Steaua Bucharest and Cluj - who he guided to the Romanian title and two domestic cups after joining midway through the 2020-21 season.

He also spent two-and-a-half years in charge of Romania, guiding them to the last 16 of Euro 2024, where they were beaten by the Netherlands.

Iordanescu takes over a Watford side currently three points above the relegation zone, having won only four of their 16 games so far.

Watford will be Iordanescu's first job in English football

Although untried in English football, Watford are getting a trophy-winning head coach with a wide-ranging CV spanning spells in his homeland, Bulgaria and Poland, as well as elite-level international experience with Romania.

His connections with his national side run deep as the son of his country's legendary former head coach Anghel Iordanescu, who famously took them to the quarter-finals of the 1994 World Cup during a reign of more than 100 games.

It is likely he will need every bit of that nous and inspiration as he becomes the latest boss to try to revive a club which continues to plough through managers at an alarming rate.

Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, with Iordanescu becoming the sixth permanent boss since Tom Cleverley was sacked in May 2025.

The Hornets' slow start to the season - with only four home wins and one point out of 24 away - has played out against the backdrop of uncertainty and unrest off the pitch.

Watford's owner, Gino Pozzo, is currently standing trial in Spain as one of a number of defendants accused of tax offences relating to Spanish team Granada, a club he used to be associated with.

He denies the allegations, which are related to player trading at Granada.

The case continues a tumultuous period for the club, with supporter and former owner Elton John voicing his frustration after a 4-0 home defeat by Burnley last month.

Fans have also questioned the running of the club, with one supporters' group declaring a loss of confidence in the ownership.

Iordanescu's immediate concern will be improving results, particularly Watford's form on the road, where they have yet to win and have conceded 18 goals in eight matches - with only Burnley letting in more.

He arrives with a reputation for defensive organisation and stability, of which the Hornets are in desperate need.

Geoff Doyle, BBC Three Counties Radio sports editor

So Watford try again with a new head coach - it is a regular occurrence at Vicarage Road.

Iordanescu has a decent CV with his work overseas in Romania, Bulgaria and Poland and is well thought of as a coach and manager.

But a lack of Championship experience is a concern and he is thrown in at the deep end with his new team hovering just above the relegation zone and confidence and morale low.

Iordanescu needs to hit the ground running in a critical week with the Hornets up against mid-table Blackburn and then Derby who are in the relegation zone.

#720. Lincoln sack head coach duo Cohen and Shaw after only six months

Chris Cohen (left) and Tom Shaw had been on the coaching staff together at Lincoln for a number of years before they got the top job together

Lincoln City have sacked their head coaches Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw just six months after they took joint charge of the Championship side.

The pair departed a little over 12 hours after they oversaw a 4-0 defeat at fellow strugglers Charlton Athletic on Tuesday.

The loss leaves the Imps just three points above the relegation places in what is the club's first season back in the second tier for 65 years.

Cohen and Shaw were assistant coaches under Michael Skubala when Lincoln were promoted as League One title winners last season.

They were surprisingly promoted to replace their boss as a managerial double act.

Championship survival behind sackings - Imps CEO

What next for Lincoln City after coach duo exit?

The duo oversaw just four wins from 17 league games this season, and Tuesday's loss at The Valley was their fifth in succession and heaviest since being thumped 6-0 by West Ham in mid-October.

Lincoln's chairman Ron Fowler, the American billionaire who took a controlling stake in the club when they were on their way to promotion last season, said the decision to sack the pair was in the "best interests" of the Imps.

"We have worked incredibly hard to reach the Championship and will do everything in our power to retain our status in this division," he told the club website., external

First-team coach Shaun Pearson will take charge of Lincoln, with the support of Paul McShane and David Preece, on an interim basis.

Lincoln are next in action on Saturday when they host high-flying Wolves.

When Cohen and Shaw got the job at Sincil Bank it came somewhat as a shock because managing football teams in tandem is somewhat of a curiosity in the game.

Liverpool famously did with Gerard Houllier and Roy Evans in 1998 when the partnership lasted six months as results slumped, while Tottenham gave it a go with Doug Livermore and Ray Clemence earlier that same decade.

The hope was that the Cohen-Shaw show would be a lot more like Coventry's success story under John Sillett and George Curtis, who guided the Sky Blues to FA Cup glory in 1987.

Lincoln's decision-makers were proactive in talking up their decision, with sporting director Jez George explaining in June that the appointment "wasn't a case of do the easy thing, but it was absolutely the right thing for the club".

Shaw and Cohen were also quizzed at length about how the joint role would work, starting with "who's going to make the subs?"

Cohen was upfront when he said "from the outside looking in, it's not normal", but the former Nottingham Forest and West Ham midfielder insisted that the job share was "really normal" to them.

How peculiar it might have looked, or how the dynamics between the pair worked, all become somewhat irrelevant in recent weeks as Lincoln's dire run of form has plunged them towards the relegation places.

Pre-match, post-match and topical Imps content

Lincoln City fans always thought this season would be tough and that they'd lose more than they win, but it was the manner of the performances recently that was most concerning.

Strange team selections in the past two matches in particular, including playing left-back Adam Reach as a right winger against Charlton Athletic in their final match in charge, was always going to raise questions, especially when the results didn't go their way, and that has ultimately been the case.

The appointment of Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw was going to be seen as a risk - joint managers/head coaches very rarely work and add in the lack of managerial experience, especially at this level.

First-team coach Shaun Pearson, who only recently joined the club , now has the task to try to turn a team low on confidence, low on ideas and low on belief into one that can stop one of the promotion favourites in Wolves on Saturday lunchtime.

Whoever's next in the dugout, however, won't come in with a massive jump in expectations of a climb up the table.

Imps supporters will be more than happy to just see their side secure a second season in the Championship.
