This projector is a handy, budget-priced tool for educating young stargazers, especially when it comes to teaching them about constellations. It’s easy to use and offers excellent image quality for its size — it’s just disappointing the selection of slides is so limited.

Requires three AA batteries (not included)

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I didn’t expect much as I unboxed the Brainstorm Night Sky; after all, I’m significantly older than this educational star projector’s target audience. Perhaps I’d come away with a sense of wonder and delight, coupled with mild irritation at having to hunt down three AA batteries to power it.

Instead, I was filled with envy as the Brainstorm Night Sky reminded me just what I was missing, thanks to the rigors of light pollution. A few minutes after powering it down, I was already making plans for my first dark sky trip, yearning for a view that rivaled the Brainstorm’s cosmic images.

Draw the curtains, press the Night Sky’s single button (tilting the projector and twisting the focus as appropriate) and it projects a circular image onto a ceiling or wall. Press the button again and the projection slowly begins to rotate, slowly but stutter-free. It really is that simple to operate and, aimed at budding astronomers aged eight or above, it's reasonably lightweight without feeling flimsy.

Weight: 14.8 oz (420 g)Bulb type: Non-specifiedLaser: NoControl: On-unitRotation: Yes, one speedProjection area: Up to 8.2 ft (2.5 m)Sleep timer: Yes (30 mins)Power: 3x AA batteries Speaker: No

I was initially a little surprised by the size of the projection: at up to 8.2 feet (2.5 m) wide it’s not going to fill an entire ceiling. It also switches off after 30 minutes, a limit that can’t be disabled, so if you’re looking to put on your own space-themed party this is not the projector for you. But it’s on point for home education and, priced from $49.99, the Brainstorm Night Sky projector won’t break the bank.

There’s minimal distortion around the edge of the images; the planets are spherical from the word go, unlike some projectors where I’ve had to tweak them to stop Mars turning into an egg. And I never once had to crane my neck because half the solar system had been projected onto a bookcase.

The Brainstorm Night Sky model I tested comes with four slides, each with a case to protect them from smudges and sticky fingers. You place one into the provided slide housing then insert that into the projector. There’s the moon, the solar system, and two showing the Northern Hemisphere’s night sky, as seen from Hawaii (a key location for astronomy).

I can appreciate the educational value of the first couple, even if I am still seething at Pluto being demoted back in 2006. But it was the latter pair of slides that really opened my eyes to what I could be seeing over my head.

I can spot maybe 10-20 stars from my backyard, cloud cover permitting; thanks to light pollution, that’s it. Even though the best stargazing apps can show me what I should see, when I step outside, all I typically see with the naked eye is the odd pinprick in the void.

But as soon as I inserted that third slide, a striking stellar display appeared above my head, with more stars than I could hope to count. Even knowing that Hawaii’s night sky stretches far further than eight feet across, the difference between this view and the one from my house was like night and day. Brainstorm claims this slide features over 20,000 stars, though that’s likely referring to the source photo rather than the projected image.

The fourth slide — the same crisp starscape but with every visible constellation labelled — was almost as attention-grabbing. Educational value aside, it drove home that I couldn’t see the majority of these star patterns to name them, my local night sky is that polluted.

Knowing what I was missing out on made me determined to take my stargazing further afield. Some of the best smart telescopes can lessen the impact of light pollution, but stepping away from skyglow is the most effective option. Hawaii’s a little far to travel, but I’ve already started looking into local dark sky sites. I just need to grab a pair of the best binoculars for stargazing, hop on my bike and I’m ready to go.

The Brainstorm Night Sky’s projections are crisp enough that you can easily make out every constellation name, but they could be a hair brighter. The Ainael Meter Galaxy Projector, for example, delivers more illumination.

If you want to use the Brainstorm Night Sky to relax, the rotate function gives its projections an oddly hypnotic effect, and the device is whisper-quiet to boot. And while Brainstorm doesn’t specify battery life, one set of rechargeables lasted me for several days.

Unfortunately, the Brainstorm Night Sky's slide collection is a little limited. There are two models, a blue version with four slides (the one I tested) and a gray version with six slides (featuring additional space shuttle and black hole images). The included instructions state you can purchase an additional slide disc showing the Southern Hemisphere’s stars, but that’s a maximum of seven images. Nor is this projector compatible with the slides from the Brainstorm Deep Sky Projector

It’s a little disappointing given that Brainstorm has clearly put thought into the projector’s educational value. Those instructions double as a poster of the solar system, and children can use a “secret code” (printed on the instructions) to explore more astronomy facts on the company’s website.

Offering extra slide packs, of the kind you can buy for the Pococo Galaxy Projector, would give it more long-term appeal. As is, I can see its novelty and educational value diminishing over time, at which point you can upgrade to one of the best star projectors.

If you’re not bothered by the lack of expandability, the Brainstorm Night Sky’s price, image quality and ease of use still make it a useful tool for kindling a child’s interest in astronomy, or as a budget-friendly gift for junior stargazers. It’s certainly spurred me into action — how much is a plane ticket to Hawaii, anyway?

#675. NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet.

The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus.

This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera.

Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains.

Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers).

While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported.

In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material.

The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past.

By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

#673. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

Marvel Studios’ first Avengers film since 2019 is less than a month away, and it might be the big-screen team-up event we thought impossible only ten years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday just landed, and it finally puts the spotlight on our boy Steve Rogers.

Avengers: Doomsday has been promising the scale and excitement the MCU has often been lacking since the Infinity Saga. Previous trailers played it safe, mostly setting up the conflict and introducing Victor Von Doom. Now it’s time for one last explosive look at the film before it tries to conquer cinemas next month.

Disney and Marvel Studios have just released a "final trailer" that puts the focus back on Steve Rogers — no longer Captain America but still ready to use Mjolnir — and Thor as the veterans leading the New Avengers, former colleagues, the Fantastic Four, and even Fox's X-Men (after some first-encounter fights, of course) against Doom and his followers.

A few dodgy CG shots aside, it looks grand, and if you're a big X-Men fan, it's hard not to get goosebumps when Cyclops (James Marsden) finally gets to say the thing.

The multiverse-spanning story is still largely kept a secret in this trailer, but at least we get a better sense of what the emotional stakes are for Rogers and how all these heroes can realistically work together against the greatest threat they've faced so far (even if most of them won't get more than a few lines).

As for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, this isn't his trailer, but the mysterious Latverian witches — who have fueled many theories online for months — are finally seen in motion.

Doom has, however, received a simple but evocative poster that mirrors one of the original Iron Man ones. Even though Marvel Studios' honcho, Kevin Feige, has shot down the theory that this Victor Von Doom is a Tony Stark variant, you can't stop marketing from doing the obvious things, it seems. We won't complain.

Avengers: Doomsday won't fix all of the Multiverse Saga's shortcomings, but at the very least, it looks like a proper fun time with more toys being mashed together than ever before and proper stakes.

Right before Christmas, it's hard to resist such a pitch.

Avengers: Doomsday assembles on December 18, 2026, only in cinemas...Yes, it opens the same day as Dune: Part Three.

#670. Is Carly Rae Jepsen’s ‘Run Away With Me’ About to Hit the Hot 100 for the First Time After Its ‘GTA VI’ Bump?

This week's Trending Up looks at some 'GTA'-related bumps, as well as a CMA Awards-driven breakthrough.

Welcome to Billboard Pro’s Trending Up newsletter, where we take a closer look at the songs, artists, curiosities and trends that have caught the music industry’s attention. Some have come out of nowhere, others have taken months to catch on, and all of them could become ubiquitous in the blink of a TikTok clip.  Explore Carly Rae Jepsen Justice Stephen Wilson Jr. See latest videos, charts and news

This week, it’s all GTA (with a little CMAs), as we look at revived favorites from Carly Rae Jepsen and The Cars, an ascendant hit from an all-star cast, and a new artist of the year winner at age 47. Related Dolly Parton to Receive CNN Heroes Legacy Award, Miley Cyrus to Accept on Her Behalf ESSENCE Festival of Culture Moving On From New Orleans After Three Decades: 'Memories Were Made -- And So Was History' Noah Kahan Caps Epic Year With 'Live From the Great Divide' Album

It’s one of the most beloved pop songs of the past 15 years — but never one of its biggest chart hits. Carly Rae Jepsen‘s “Run Away With Me” became a cult classic almost immediately upon its single release (from her enduring E•MO•TION album) in 2015, but Billboard Hot 100 success totally eluded it in its moment. (In 2023, Billboard named it the 21st greatest pop song of the Hot 100 era to never reach the chart.) But in 2026, a great pop song still has a chance to reach the Hot 100 no matter when it was originally released — and “Run Away With Me” now has the best opportunity it’s had in a decade, thanks to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI.

“Run Away With Me” plays in the record-breaking new game during a scene when its dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, are enjoying the Vice City high life after the latter’s release from prison. With its cinematic sax and propulsive synth-pop shuffle making it an ideal soundtrack for just about any action-packed sequence, the song has become one of the breakout musical moments from the game’s heavily music-focused universe — and led many pop fans to wonder if it could result in the storied track finally reaching the Hot 100 for the first time.

The answer? Maybe — but it still has a long way to go.

The song’s streaming breakout has unquestionably been real: It was pulling daily official on-demand streams in the low 20,000s in the days before the game’s release, but that number had broken six digits by Sunday (Nov. 22, three days after GTA VI‘s release), and was all the way up to 281,000 by Monday, according to early data provided by Luminate. That’s a gain of nearly 1,100% over the total the song posted last Wednesday, just before the game’s release, but it’s still a little low for a streaming-driven-song on the Hot 100.

The question is if the song can continue its viral growth throughout this week, and maybe even into next week. It’s got a bit of a late start for this tracking week, which runs through Thursday — and as of Tuesday, the song still wasn’t streaming enough to enter the daily top 200 on either Spotify or Apple Music — so its best chance of breaching the chart might come next week, especially if it continues to grow and then stays stable, with daily U.S. streaming numbers more in the 500k-600k range.

However, it will be getting late early on the charts for songs like “Run Away With Me” by next week — since the yearly avalanche of Christmas-related titles, which has already provided a pretty heavy snowfall on the Hot 100 in November, will really hit following Thanksgiving. At that point, non-holiday-related space on the chart will become increasingly limited, and the bar that “Run” needs to clear in order to reach the listing will climb higher and higher.

It will be a challenge for “Run Away With Me” to broach the Hot 100 — but it definitely could happen, if its moment continues to spread and attract new fans while re-activating old ones. Could it get extra momentum through new TikTok trends? Will a still-unreleased remix from Overmono — featured in the game, but not yet available on streaming — end up as an important wildcard? Might pop radio belateedly decide to embrace it, in a way it never quite did a decade ago? Could its best chance of breaking the chart not actually come next week, but next year?

It’s too early to say on any of this, but one thing is for sure: Its longtime fans will be there rooting it on, supporting as much as they can and air-saxing the whole way. — ANDREW UNTERBERGER

Outside of Morgan Wallen’s “Last Thing You Need,” the all-star jam “Flower in a Hurricane” was already the closest thing to a pre-minted hit from the Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album soundtrack, having already spent multiple weeks on the Hot 100. But following the game’s release, the song from Justice, Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard has reached a new level of popularity — and may soon challenge or even eclipse even the commercially bulletproof Wallen’s latest hit single on the Hot 100.

In the four days following the game’s Nov. 19 release, “Flower’ racked up nearly 7.6 million official on-demand U.S. streams, according to early data provided by Luminate — a 165% gain over the 2.9 million streams the songs racked up over the previous Friday-Monday period (Nov. 13-16). While doing so, it also topped Spotify’s Daily Top Songs USA chart and reached No. 3 on the Apple Music realtime chart. It all portends another huge jump for “Flower” on next week week’s Hot 100, with the song already reaching a new peak of No. 45 this week, and looking to shoot into the top 20 or possibly even the top 10 next week.

But that’s not all for Justice — the French house duo also responsible for composing the game’s epic score — who has two additional new original collabs on the game’s official soundtrack. One of those, the album-opening “Starting From Zero” — a teamup with yacht rock icon Michael McDonald — is also off to a strong start on streaming, earning 1.8 million streams in its first four days of release (Nov. 20-23), and potentially pushing for an outside chance at a Hot 100 debut of its own if its numbers keep climbing. (The duo’s third GTA song, “Pusher” with Gesaffelstein, is also up 53% to 464,000 streams.)

And Wallen’s “Last Thing”? That’s up about 31% too over that four-day period — albeit with a lower streaming total now (around 6 million) than “Hurricane” — and should also be due for a chart rebound from its current No. 17 perch, possibly back to the chart’s top 10. — AU

After The Cars‘ “Drive” reached No. 3 on the Hot 100 during its initial 1984 run, the dramatic rock classic is back in the cultural mainstream following its key sync in the newly released Grand Theft Auto VI video game.

In the Friday-Monday period (Nov. 13-16) preceding the game’s Nov. 19 release, “Drive” collected 629,000 official on-demand U.S. streams. In the Friday-Monday period following the game’s release (Nov. 20-23), that total leapt 83% to over 1.15 million official on-demand U.S. streams, according to early data provided by Luminate.

Even though Rockstar Games teamed up with Atlantic Records for a gargantuan, genre-spanning, 57-song compilation soundtrack, “Drive” remained the developers’ North Star. Billboard’s latest cover story revealed that Rockstar first tried to clear “Drive” for GTA in 2002, but this year’s long-awaited sync “was a testament to the company’s unwavering prioritization of music, the relationships it has cultivated throughout the industry and the meticulous curation that has transformed Grand Theft Auto into one of the past 20 years’ most culture-saturating, riveting and lucrative products.” With first-day sales of $3.79 billion, “Drive” now soundtracks one of the biggest monocultural moments of the decade — and indeed, is the first song players hear play on the in-game radio.

“Drive” also experienced a smaller resurgence in 2019, following the death of frontman Ric Ocasek. The song returned to No. 6 on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs back then, and to No. 27 on Digital Song Sales. – KYLE DENIS

Despite being born in the 1970s, Stephen Wilson Jr. was named country music’s new artist of the year at the Country Music Awards last Wednesday (Nov. 18) — capping an incredible journey that’s taking Wilson from the science lab at Mars Inc. to songwriting rooms in Nashville, to now his own success as a solo singer-songwriter. The 47-year-old singer-songwriter was one of the biggest non-Ella Langley presences at the ceremonies, not only winning new artist of the year and giving a memorably emotional speech following the win, but also performing his new single “I’m a Song” alongside fellow country powerhouse (and 2026 CMA Award winner) Chris Stapleton.

And it seems like the awards might only be the beginning of Wilson’s mainstream breakthrough, as his streaming numbers shot through the roof following his big night. His catalog drew 8.7 million official on-demand U.S. streams over the three days following the awards (Nov. 19-21), more than tripling the under 2.9 million streams he amassed over the prior Thursday-Saturday period. The biggest gains from that period were of course reserved for “I’m a Song” (up a staggering 1,089% to 1.4 million streams), as well as his breakout cover of Ben E. King’s “Stand By Me” (up 135% to 1.1 million) and his CMA Award-nominated 2026 single “Gary” (up 281% to 753,000).

And of course, Ella Langley also saw a bump from her five wins — including for her big winners, record-breaking Hot 100 smash “Choosin’ Texas” (up 11% to 8.6 million streams) and Billboard 200-topping album Dandelion (up 16% to 24.2 million), as well as for her acoustically performed “Loving Life Again” (up 17% to 2.5 million). – AU

#669. What is the Riemann hypothesis? A guide to the famed conjecture that rules prime numbers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

German mathematician Bernhard Riemann formulated his famous conjecture in 1859.Credit: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (CC0)

On 20 November, mathematicians made two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most important open problem in mathematics.

The question had remained unanswered since it was formulated in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–66). His statement is central to the theory of prime numbers, the whole numbers that cannot be evenly divided by any other number except themselves or 1.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is important because these numbers are central to all of maths. “There is nothing more basic and more fundamental in mathematics that the prime numbers,” says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves — in a way that presages the way music recordings are compressed into mp3 files — and his hypothesis is usually described in abstruse-sounding language. But at its heart, the idea boils down to a statistical test that is familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

Nature breaks down the Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians want to know how predictable the prime numbers are. The German scientist Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who many consider to be the greatest mathematician in history, had noticed in the late 1700s (when he was a teenager) that if you pick any whole number, the odds that it’s a prime depend on the number’s size. Primes slowly become sparser as numbers become bigger. Gauss observed that their frequency seems to depend on (or, is inversely proportional to) the number of digits. Roughly speaking, among numbers with k digits, one in every k of them is a prime.

In Riemann’s time, a half-century after Gauss’s guess, there was still no rigorous proof of this. In a landmark paper in 1859, Riemann stated his belief that the late Gauss, who had been one of his mentors at the University of Göttingen, had been right.

But Riemann — who was a “daring” thinker, says maths historian Rossana Tazzioli at the University of Lille in France — went much further. He proposed that Gauss’s “one in every k” guess was a good statistical prediction, meaning that the frequency of the primes should not fluctuate away from it too much. In other words, Riemann made a guess about the margin of error of Gauss’s prediction.

If true, this ‘Riemann hypothesis’ would make primes’ behaviour similar to that of a random process, such as a series of coin tosses. More precisely, he suggested that when you count the primes among the first n whole numbers, fluctuations would take a form that many scientists are familiar with: “The idea of the Riemann hypothesis is that the error term looks a lot like √n, which is what any random model will give you,” says Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Such square-root terms pop up everywhere in data analysis, because they control the shrinking of a margin of error as the number n of data points grows.

In his paper, Riemann did much more than guess. He introduced tools that would constitute the basis for much of the work on number theory — the branch of mathematics that concerns integers, primes and divisibility — in the following centuries.

First, by developing new techniques in analysis — another word for advanced calculus — as he went along, Riemann constructed the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter ‘zeta’).

Riemann then showed that the function embodied an enormous amount of information about prime numbers. First, he proved that the solutions to the equation ζ (z) = 0 — where z is a point on a plane — encode the statistical distribution of prime numbers along the number line. To do so, Riemann employed a type of Fourier analysis, the type of maths that nowadays enables the compression of music into compact mp3 files by breaking sound waves down into sinusoidal components.

#668. A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors

Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter

The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

Materials provided by University of California - San Diego. Original written by Michelle Franklin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#667. Director Peter Berg Isn’t Giving Up on the Unreleased Rihanna Documentary: ‘Keep Hope Alive’

The director said in 2023 that he spent six and a half years filming the project.

Remember the Peter Berg-directed Rihanna documentary that was announced way back in 2016, and was reportedly sold to Amazon for $25 million in 2019?

Well, Berg is choosing to remain optimistic.

During a conversation with Complex published on Wednesday (Nov. 25), Berg — who also directed the singer and business mogul in 2012’s Battleship — discussed the doc’s current status. “There’s always hope. Keep hope alive,” he said of the unreleased documentary. “If and when it does [come out], it’s going to be a banger.”

He was talked about why he thinks the nine-time Grammy winner hasn’t done more movies, and he commended the “We Found Love” singer’s ability to always make the right decision. “Rihanna does what she wants to do. She follows her heart. She follows her creative instincts,” Berg told the publication. “When she did Battleship, she was really interested in seeing what being in a big, wild Hollywood action movie was like. And then she went and made a bunch of great albums and now she’s raising a beautiful family. I guarantee you she’s going to be back in music and it’s going to be a banger.”

Berg and his team spent years recording and piecing things together for the documentary about the star, but it’s ultimately up to Rihanna whether she wants to release it eventually. He said as much in 2023 when talking with The Hollywood Reporter. “It’s done and sold, and Amazon’s ready,” the director told the outlet at the time. “She’s a perfectionist, so we keep adding. It’s been six and a half years of filming, so, yeah, it’s ready to come out. We’re just waiting on her to say, ‘Yeah, let’s do it.’ I don’t know. Maybe it’ll be a 10-year project.”

Rihanna most recently starred in 2025’s animated film Smurfs, lending her voice to Smurfette. The last live action movie she starred in was Amazon Prime’s Guava Island opposite Donald Glover, though she makes a cameo in Ali G: Who Iz I?, which arrived in October.

These strange geological features may offer clues to the Red Planet's watery past.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

Data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

The rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of New Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! You can follow her on Twitter @Sam_Ashley13.

#665. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#664. Luke Bryan & Luke Combs Channel Old-School Influences in ‘Finders Keepers’: ‘I Want to Put Songs Out That Could Go Right Into The Set List’

Billboard's Makin' Tracks column looks at the writing and recording behind the Luke Bryan and Luke Combs collaboration "Finders Keepers."

“Luke-ing” back across the years, Luke Bryan didn’t have much country competition in branding his name.

Hank Williams recorded a series of recitations under the pseudonym Luke the Drifter, and stretching the boundaries a bit, Waylon Jennings had a landmark hit with “Luckenbach, Texas (Back to the Basics of Love).” Bryan got used to being known in the genre by a single syllable until a “Hurricane” hit in 2016.

“I thought I had the Luke name,” Bryan says. “I thought I had that solidly before Luke Combs. I mean, the disc jockeys could just say, ‘That was Luke.’ They didn’t have to verify last names.” Related Dolly Parton to Receive CNN Heroes Legacy Award, Miley Cyrus to Accept on Her Behalf ESSENCE Festival of Culture Moving On From New Orleans After Three Decades: 'Memories Were Made -- And So Was History' Noah Kahan Caps Epic Year With 'Live From the Great Divide' Album Explore Luke Bryan Luke Combs See latest videos, charts and news

Not that Bryan has a problem with the situation. In fact, he enlisted Combs as a feature voice on “Finders Keepers,” released by Row Crop/MCA Nashville to country radio via PlayMPE on Oct. 12. It lists on Billboard’s Country Airplay as “Luke Bryan & Luke Combs,” though Bryan doesn’t particularly care how people refer to them.

“Luke Squared,” he says, “whatever you want to call it.”

The song’s writers were just happy they got the call. Bryan heard it — and recorded it — 15 days after its official date of creation when his manager, KP Entertainment founder/president Kerri Edwards, was going through unopened emails during Bryan’s session at Nashville’s Ocean Way on March 6. She played it for Bryan and his producers, Jeff and Jody Stevens, during their drive to Dicey’s Tavern on a lunch break, and they added it to that afternoon’s material. The musicians picked it up easily.

“They ran through it one time, and ran through it another time, and that was it,” Jeff recalls.

Songwriter Sam Ellis (“What If I Never Get Over You,” “More Hearts Than Mine”) hosted the writing session that spawned “Finders Keepers” on Feb. 19 at his East Nashville studio. When the initial song ideas fell flat for Ellis and his co-writers, Jimi Bell (“Backup Plan,” “Last Night Lonely”) and Beau Bailey (“Stay Country or Die Tryin’,” “Favorite Country Song”), Bailey apologetically mentioned a hook he’d concocted during a brainstorming exercise: “Finders keepers, losers drinkers.” No apology was necessary; his co-writers loved the wordplay.

“They just went to town,” Bailey says, “They’re lyrical and musical assassins.”

They had chatted up their passion for Dwight Yoakam at the start of the appointment, and they used the pace of Yoakam’s “Suspicious Minds” cover, from the 1992 Honeymoon in Vegas soundtrack, as a template for “Finders Keepers.”

“I’m a huge Dwight Yoakam fan, so that was 100% channeled that day,” Bell says. “As soon as he said that title, I kind of heard a Dwight Yoakam thing in my mind.”

They sketched out the musical framework for it, ensuring that the chorus would start in an energetic place. It was obvious that the plot needed to address a broken heart, and the song’s second line, “Made a home in that hole you dug,” acknowledged the protagonist blew it. “You do know it’s his fault,” Ellis says, “and you’re kind of on his side.”

They doubled down on the breakup a few lines later with “She took the ‘U’ right out of ‘us,’” though the twist in that phrase may escape most listeners until they see the lyrics in print.

“It’s always fun when you can sneak a little bit of smartness into a happy, full-on, go-lucky drinking song,” Bailey notes. “Then when you dissect it, you’re like, ‘Wait, this actually makes sense. We haven’t heard it said like this.’”

They introduced the “Finders keepers, losers drinkers” hook in amped-up fashion to start the chorus, though returning to that hook for the payoff presented a challenge. Those four words worked better as a set up for the last line, which ultimately became a consolation prize for the guy on his barstool: “Hey man, at least the beer is cold.”

The chorus ended that way for a bit, but as they worked with it further, it called out for more. So they tacked a post-chorus line onto the cold beer: “So grab you one, the night is good, and the night is young.” That phrase came with three-part harmony, performed mostly over a heavy kick drum, a la Alabama’s “Mountain Music.” The second time around, the post-chorus grew even longer, as the Alabama section focused on the hot girls dancing: “Don’t look now, one’s lookin’ your way.”

“I love just having those dualities,” Bell says, “turning what otherwise would have been a kind of a sad situation into a party song.”

Bell sang lead for the demo, produced by Ellis with an instrumental break featuring an electric guitar that handed off the back half of the solo to a steel guitar. They thought the song was a winner — that Alabama-styled post-chorus cinched it — and Bell’s publisher, Worktape Music owner/operator Travis Gordon, envisioned it for Bryan. When Edwards played it for her artist, Bryan was won over by the Alabama sound. “It’s kind of a little cherry on top at the end of the chorus,” he says.

Returning from lunch, Bryan’s creative team made some small changes to the demo’s arrangement, particularly for the final chorus, where Jeff Stevens reworked the chord structure. “They had gone to a chord progression that, to me, didn’t feel like it contributed to the energy level that it should be at that point in the song,” he says.

They went back to the original chords and had drummer Miles McPherson — working his first Bryan session — deaden cymbal crashes with his hands to create a power sound. They brought fiddler Joe Spivey into Sound Emporium to enhance the old-school country sound, though Spivey was hesitant to play anything outside of long notes, since the original band had already filled up much of the space.

“It just felt like it was slowing it down,” Jody says. “It needed some fiddle parts that moved with the rhythm of the song.”

Jody dictated some simmering passages, and Spivey nailed it within 10 minutes. Bryan’s tracking-day vocals weren’t where he wanted them — “I had come off the road,” he says, “and I sounded like a coyote caught in a bear trap” — but he knocked out the final version in a date at Blackbird Studios.

Next up, background vocalist Trey Keller mirrored the demo’s original harmonies, but Jeff had him redo the part, creating more of a Ricky Skaggs bluegrass tone. All of those pieces were in place when Bryan sent “Finders Keepers” to Combs, who agreed immediately to sing on it. Jeff and Jody recorded him at producer-engineer Chip Matthews’ studio in three short takes.

“We couldn’t have been in there more than about 30 minutes for vocals,” Jody says.

Edwards later played it for Bell and Ellis in person, and they flipped out when they heard Combs emerge on verse two — they’d not projected it as a collaboration. The Luke Squared dueling voices made it a likely radio release, but Ellis also hoped to hear it outside the bars on Nashville’s Lower Broadway.

“I wanted this thing to sound like downtown, where you’re walking by and you can hear a band in the distance playing it,” he says. “That’s something you want to hear cruising down Broadway, you know, chicken picking and all that stuff.”

It’s working well on radio, positioned at No. 30 on the Country Airplay chart dated Nov. 28. And Bryan is focused on its concert benefits, too.

“I’m really in an uptempo mood these days,” he says. “I want to put songs out that could go right into the set list for my tours and really add a lot of energy.”

#663. France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency

Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

Before New Shepard all boosters were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever.

After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground. This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history.

The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.

Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms.

But in the end, Blue Origin did it first.

Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket.

Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company announced a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects.

But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown.

Blue Origin has since reflown a New Glenn booster, and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance.

#660. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.
