#659. Lucy Vives, Sofia Monroy, OKAN, Moy Bobadilla & More Emerging Latin Artists on Our Radar

Here are the rising stars we've discovered in November, and who should be on your radar.

Every month, Billboard Latin and Billboard Español editors spotlight a group of rising artists whose music we love. Think “diamantes en bruto,” or “diamonds in the rough.” These are newcomers who have yet to impact the mainstream — but whose music excites us, and who we believe our readers should make a point to discover. Explore Billboard See latest videos, charts and news

Our latest edition of On the Radar Latin includes a wave of emerging artists, who we discovered by scrolling on social media, networking, or coming across their music at a showcase, for example. See our November 2026 recommendations below. Related Dolly Parton to Receive CNN Heroes Legacy Award, Miley Cyrus to Accept on Her Behalf ESSENCE Festival of Culture Moving On From New Orleans After Three Decades: 'Memories Were Made -- And So Was History' Noah Kahan Caps Epic Year With 'Live From the Great Divide' Album

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: Earlier this year, Colombian artist Pipe Bueno teamed up with Cumbia Pedregal on “Dime Que Me Hiciste” — a winning blend of smooth, irresistibly-catchy cumbia with a distinct sound. Made up of brothers Emilio, José Pablo, and Luche Zepeda, this trio feels like a band of old souls reincarnated in 2026 with influences from pop, banda grupera, and regional Mexican music, among others. The more I listened to their music, the more I discovered elements of 1980s Latin America: long hair, colorful suits, and soft vocals that seem to sigh through the verses.

Grupo Pedregal’s musical and visual style stands out amid today’s hard-hitting, rhythmic sounds — embracing love songs, heartbreak and clean lyrics rooted in the timeless spirit of Mexican music. In May, the group released its debut album, Sabor a Llanto, featuring “Mi Peor Apuesta,” its second collaboration with singer-songwriter Eden Muñoz (following 2025’s “Sin Ti No Sé Vivir”). — INGRID FAJARDO

Song for Your Playlist: “Que Se Pudra El Amor”

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: When I first discovered Cuba’s reparto music, one of the first artists that captured by attention, mainly because of his lyrical content, was El Dukesito. With songs such as “La Oportunidad” and “Voy A Mi” — songs that are rooted in personal growth and potent affirmations, rather than the common provocative and street slang that characterizes the genre — I knew he was a special breed.

Born Nassir Cristo Duquesne Dublón in La Habana, the Miami-based artist dubs himself as “el más completo y versátil de la nueva” (the most complete and versatile artist of the new generation) — and his “No Llores Por El,” a ranchera-tinged pop song released this year with Bambino the Boss attests to that. With his crystalline vocals, the 30-year-old artist, who’s signed to Rami Récords, has received the stamp of approval from Cuban pioneers including Gente de Zona, Chocolate MC, and Wow Popy. Dukesito is currently making the rounds with his new singles “Solo Solito” and “Tu No Sientes” with Yeyo Pa’ Que Sepa — both released under Plus Media. — JESSICA ROIZ

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: Throughout this year, Eley Romero has demonstrated that he possesses all the qualities needed to transition from an emerging talent to a star of the new generation of Mexican music, with a repertoire centered on songs about love. In May 2026, he signed with La Empresa Music, which significantly boosted his streaming numbers — his tracks have now amassed over 74 million plays, at the time of publishing. One of these, “Qué Se Siente” — a collaboration with Adrián L. Santos — proved to be a turning point in his career, drawing the attention of major artists within the genre, such as Kane Rodríguez, Los Chavalitos, and Los 2 de La S. Born in Los Mochis, Sinaloa, the artist— who is also a songwriter — recently released the track “¿Cómo Le Digo A Mi Amá?” alongside Los Primos del Este. Looking ahead to early 2027, he has a series of significant collaborations lined up with El Rabanito, Raúl Beltrán and Efecto Elegante, which will mark another major milestone in his career. — TERE AGUILERA

Song for Your Playlist: “Qué Se Siente” feat. Adrián L. Santos

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: Powered by her wistful and seductive vocals, Lucy Vives gives life her debut EP called cimiento. The five-track project released earlier this month via M3 Records brings to the forefront her progressive project that’s rooted in an indie-alternative-pop realm with an intimate, vulnerable, and imaginative storytelling. Each song is penned by the Colombian-Puerto Rican artist herself, further making each song personal and relatable. “This first EP was a deeply introspective journey for me, one that ultimately became something like a book of short stories. Several of the songs are little stories of their own, and to me, this project is an introduction, a beginning for me and my music,” she explains in a press statement. An emerging act in her own right, the 30-year-old singer-songwriter first arrived on the Billboard charts in 2021 when the tropical “Besos En Cualquier Horario” in collab with Carlos Vives (her father) and Mau y Ricky reached No. 10 on the Latin Pop Airplay chart. — J.R.

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: In October, I went to see Grupo Firme perform at Guadalajara’s Palenque during the Día de Muertos celebrations. While I was backstage, I came across a tall young man wearing a white shirt, cowboy boots, and a black cowboy hat, who was accompanied by his parents. His charm and cheerful, ambitious energy were immediately apparent. His name was Moisés “Moy” Bobadilla Martínez, one of Firme’s surprise guests, who was born in 2001 in Santa María de los Ángeles, Jalisco.

Midway through Grupo Firme’s set that October night, Moy joined Eduin Caz for a duet of “Corazón,” then performed one of his solo songs called “Tus Mentiras.” I was struck not only by his voice and impressive high notes, but also by his commanding stage presence. In a venue where the stage feels so close to the audience, his presence made an even greater impact because of the way the place is set up. Following that performance, Moy had several key shows, including at the Plaza de Toros in Mexico City, Domo Care in Monterrey, Palenque de Querétaro, and more. Bobadilla’s latest single is called “Del Temu” in collaboration with Luis Mexia. — I.F.

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: With a joyous blend of Afro-Cuban roots with jazz, classical music and global rhythms, OKAN has been gaining recognition in North America, performing on stages like the Lincoln Center, the Kennedy Center and the Montreal Jazz Festival, as well as NPR’s Tiny Desk. Comprised of vocalists and multi-instrumentalists Elizabeth Rodríguez and Magdelys Savigne, who were born and raised in Cuba and now live between Toronto and Miami, this two-time JUNO Award-winning, Grammy-nominated duo just released its fourth studio album, Ife Ara (Yoruba for “self-love”) under Lulaworld Records, expanding their musical vocabulary with contemporary, more commercial sounds including reparto, trap, Latin pop and electronic music. — SIGAL RATNER-ARIAS

Song For Your Playlist: “Te Falta Grasa” feat. Daymé Arocena

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: After writing or co-writing hits for artists such as Alejandro Sanz, Danny Ocean, Fonseca and Ca7riel & Paco Amoroso, Venezuelan songwriter Santander made his debut as a singer this year under Universal Music Latino, proving that his voice and presence are well worth seeing and hearing. His initial releases (“Peliculear,” “Once Again” and “Full En Serio”) feature a poetic narrative, a pleasing, velvety tone and a fusion of Latin and global rhythms that’s highly commercial. With credits on proven hits like “Imagínate” by Danny Ocean and Kapo (which reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Latin Airplay chart — and Tropicalia by Fonseca (winner of the Latin Grammy for best contemporary tropical album) Santander is emerging as one of the most promising new voices in today’s Latin music scene. — S.R.A.

Why They Should Be on Your Radar: Born in Mexico City and raised in Sweden, Sofia Monroy spent years figuring out how to reconcile her two cultural identities through music. She initially wrote songs in English before incorporating Spanish when, as she put it, “something’s missing.” Drawing from the Swedish pop and Latin rhythms she grew up with, Monroy has carved out a multilingual strain of alternative pop that moves fluidly between Spanish, English and Swedish. “It’s just a culture clash, but that’s me at the end of the day,” she told Billboard Español at Billboard Brasil and Meta’s Latin Grammy-week activation.

While her 2025 debut, Morena, introduced that evolving identity, her more introspective 2026 sophomore album, WO[E]MAN, explores how women are perceived, judged and defined by others. Its standout “Pegadito” showcases Monroy’s knack for pairing emotional tension with rhythmic finesse. For the Latin Grammy best new artist nominee, finding her voice ultimately meant embracing the plurality of her upbringing. “I don’t have to choose,” she said. “I can do both.” — ISABELA RAYGOZA

#658. How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work

How realistic are the zero-g sports we see in sci-fi? We talk to Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, to find out.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics. The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation, the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut.

Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field.

As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play.

We rarely think about it in an Earth context, but every sport is heavily influenced by gravity. It defines how balls arc, how quickly players can move, and even how we orient ourselves in play spaces. Remove the gravity, and all of those assumptions and mechanics evaporate as well.

"First of all, in zero g, Isaac Newton will win every time," Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, told Space. Les is a physicist with over 35 years of experience working at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, as well as a science fiction author.

"'For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction,'" quotes Johnson. "This is very difficult to simulate in real life due to gravity; special effects often try to compensate. With today’s AI and green screens, it can actually look good on screen."

In a microgravity scenario, the concept of up and down is no longer relevant. Suddenly, the playing field expands from a single, fixed plane to a fully three-dimensional space that includes height.

Momentum is also a completely different beast. Instead of being able to quickly stop and pivot the way you can during terrestrial sports, once you start moving in microgravity, you keep going until something stops you. It takes the trickiness of moving on ice in sports like hockey and increases it by several orders of magnitude.

Of course, the havoc wouldn't stop with maneuvering yourself. Any ball or other object would also be subject to this altered set of physics.

As Johnson points out, "Aside from maneuvering the body and not tumbling or going in the wrong direction, the most difficult part would probably be throwing or hitting a ball in zero g. There would be no arc, just a straight-line throw. That would take getting used to doing, given that we’ve spent our entire lives calculating how high and fast to throw a ball in 1G so it gets to the person we intend."

Science fiction interpretations have often leaned into these differences; in many cases, low-g sports look more like three-dimensional chess than the highly physical contests we're used to here on Earth.

Ironically, many of the best examples of space-based sports are the most grounded, where real-world physics are fully accounted for.

2013's "Ender's Game" gives us one of the best examples of a zero-g arena in space. Dubbed the "Battle Room," it's a giant hollow cube filled with obstacles. Teams enter through gates at opposite ends and participate in laser tag-style drills while having to grapple with three-dimensional space, while also finding ways to propel and protect themselves.

"The Battle Room sequence does a great job of thinking about straight‑line, constant‑velocity motion," Johnson said. "No 'reaction' to slow you down or change your direction. Characters push off walls or each other, then drift until they hit something or fire their suit's thrusters."

Johnson said Ender's Game also did an admirable job of showcasing how alternate physics require another layer of planning when moving through space.

"They went to great lengths to show that there was no preferred 'up' or 'down'. Again, very accurate and realistic thinking. Floating obstacles in the battle space created realistic constraints: if you don't think about where you'll rebound, you can pin yourself behind an obstacle or drift out of the fight."

Recognizing how important play can be (and, perhaps, acknowledging ways to combat the lingering specter of space madness), real-world space agencies have begun brainstorming what recreation in low gravity might look like. Some proposed ideas include 3D ball games not wholly dissimilar from the Battle Room, where players enter a cube or spherical arena and push off walls/pass a ball in any direction, scoring by hitting targets.

Elastic tethers are another experimental concept being bandied around, where players are connected to flexible tethers to improve movement control and cut down on collisions. The Space Games Federation has also floated the idea of a version of space basketball, where the goal is guiding a magnetic ball through hoops, as well as some version of space dodgeball.

Of course, these proposals are nothing more than thought exercises at the moment. We're a long way out from vast human populations living in zero-g environments for extended periods of time, and even further still from building spaceships capable of housing a sports hall.

NASA astronauts have experimented with trying to play various terrestrial sports in space, usually aboard the International Space Station. We've seen them playing soccer, lacrosse, and hockey with varying degrees of success.

These fun experiments mainly serve to prove what we've already suspected: that terrestrial sports can't be directly translated into a zero-g environment. We'll need new rules, arenas, and whole new games if we're going to make any headway with competitive sports in space.

Sci-fi has a pretty good track record for simulating open 3D environments in microgravity. The genre also tends to do fairly well in depicting the methodical pace of moving through space and how that would affect competition (and combat).

Games like "Echo Arena" even use technology to help simulate these factors. Echo Arena is a VR game where you boost around a zero-g arena, punching opponents and trying to toss a disc into a goal.

The game's innovative movement system allows players to grab almost any surface, either moving themselves along it or pushing off to float in a given direction. Players are also given wrist-mounted thrusters to let them course-correct a little, offering a respite from the unforgiving laws of motion.

Dead Space also has a section that functions similarly but with conventional game controls, though the only sport there is "don't get eaten by necromorphs."

With that said, there are areas where sci-fi portrayals of zero-G games fall down. Energy levels and fatigue is a big one: constant maneuvering with your arms is exhausting, which is why real astronauts rely heavily on handholds. In a similar vein, there's the issue of infinite momentum, specifically as it applies to rotation.

Johnson specifically quibbles with scenes in the Ender's Game Battle Room and "how quickly the participants can rotate their bodies or part of their bodies without going into an uncontrollable spin." He points to incidents where real-life astronauts have demonstrated how challenging this phenomenon would actually be. "I’ve watched many videos of astronauts on the ISS twist and then bounce off the wall or something. They have all looked very clumsy when they do this."

The other kind of space constraints are also often hand-waved. Even the largest existing spacecraft pale in comparison to the size of stadiums or arenas on Earth. Our early attempts at space-based sports will likely have to be centered in much smaller playing areas.

Safety issues are frequently downplayed as well; colliding with metal surfaces at high speeds in enclosed environments risks serious bodily harm to players as well as potential damage to suits/gear.

With that said, newer sci-fi portrayals are getting closer to reality by emphasizing slower, more deliberate movement and placing the focus on strategic thinking rather than athletic prowess.

In the meantime, astronauts might have to stick to video games to scratch their competitive itches.

Alan Bradley is an experienced tech and culture writer with more than 20 years covering gaming, tech, and hardware. His work has appeared in Rolling Stone, U.S. News & World Report, PCMag, TechRadar, GamesRadar+, CNET, Live Science, Variety, and many other outlets.

#657. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle."

Materials provided by University of Wollongong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#655. Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire

Human rights groups have slammed plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. In other news, business start-ups in Germany are on track to reach the highest level since 2015.

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war."

The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing."

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts."

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk said he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges."

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."

It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."

Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

#654. Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer."

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries."

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:

"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as important as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago."

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

#653. Here’s How to Find Rick Ross’ Mansion in ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’

The Miami rapper took to social media and urged fans to find his house in the game's fictionalized version of South Florida.

You can visit Rick Ross‘ Miami mansion in Grand Theft Auto VI.

The rapper took to his Instagram Story and encouraged fans and gamers to find his home in the game and to send him proof in the DMs when they do. “Who can pull up, Vice City, pull up to Star Island and see the muthaf—kin BOAT?” he asked fans in a video. “And everybody that’s playing GTA VI right now, DM it to me when you pull up on Star Island and I need to see if you muthaf—kin see the biggest. The BOAT of all time.” Players can search for Ross’ house on Starfish Island, Grand Theft Auto‘s version of Star Island where many celebrities have property in real life.

YouTuber M3RKMUS1C made a 12-minute tutorial showing gamers the exact location of not only Rozay’s pad but The Weeknd‘s as well, who posted a picture of the Vice City version of his estate on his gene.hackerman finsta recently. He starts his video off by heading straight there. You can find the Toronto singer’s mansion in the Peacock Estates, just south of Peacock Bay, located in the South Vice-Dade County area. He then heads to Starfish Island where he visits Rick Ross’ mansion, which is located on the northeastern side of the island (you can’t miss it), and immediately encounters one of the rarest cars in the game. We don’t want to spoil which specific car it is, so check out the tutorial if you’re curious.

Both Rick Ross and The Weeknd have music that you can hear on the game’s many radio stations, while The Weeknd also contributed original music for the main score on Justice’s song “My Only Vice,” which the streets (social media) are saying plays an important role in the game. You can check out an in-depth look at how the game’s score and soundtrack came together in Billboard‘s cover story.

Why are arteries spared? This mystery is investigated by Sabata et al.4 in their paper in Nature.

#650. Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

The discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

"Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," said Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean

The discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

The clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details

Scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

The team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

"Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," said Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities."

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives

The rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the new flagship research vessel David Packard.

MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

#649. Publishing Briefs: Believe & GL Music Form JV, Gram Parsons to Be Administered by Peermusic

Plus, Tiësto collaborator at Electric Feel Publishing EU and more publishing news and signings.

Believe Music Publishing and GL Music Entertainment have formed a joint venture, which sees Believe Music Publishing administering GL Music Entertainment’s catalog.

GL Music Entertainment was founded by Kim Nowak-Zorde, Daniel Fält and Lasse Lindorff, who also all work as songwriters and producers. Lindorff serves as the company’s CEO, Nowak-Zorde as head of entertainment and Christan Fløe Svenningsen is publishing director. Artists on the company’s roster has written and produced songs for Kylie Minogue, BTS, Julie Bergan and more. GL Music largely works with K-pop, J-pop and C-pop.

“The partnership with Believe Music Publishing gives us the global infrastructure, an even stronger international network and resources to take that ambition to another level, while allowing GL Music Entertainment to remain independent, entrepreneurial and creatively focused.”

Pete McCamley, who serves as vp of publishing at Believe, said, “Having worked with GL Music Entertainment from a distance for many years, I am delighted to work much closer with Lasse & Christian through our new venture. They have built a great creative business that operates on songwriter-first principles, with an incredibly strong track record across territories and genres. I’m excited to see the results of this new collaboration and be part of this next chapter.”

Chris Meehan, CEO of publishing at Believe, added, “Lasse, Kim and Christian always put songwriters first, and you can feel that in everything GL Music Entertainment does. Their writers have made their mark everywhere from the Nordics to K-pop, and we’re excited to give that talent even more reach through our global network. I’m really looking forward to seeing what we can achieve together.” — Ariel King

See more publishing news and signings below.

Peermusic will begin administering the catalog of Gram Parsons, the company announced. The country rocker passed away in 1973 at age 26, but his musical works continued to inspire artists including Emmylou Harris, Elvis Costello and Margo Price

“My father’s music has always had a life of its own, reaching across generations and continuing to inspire artists and listeners in ways I don’t think even he could have imagined,” Polly Parsons said in a statement. “It means so much to me to help preserve that legacy while also finding ways for new people to discover his songs.  His music was never bound by genre or convention, and I think that’s why it still resonates so deeply. My hope is that this new partnership will not only honor the incredible body of work he left behind but also introduce his music to a whole new generation of fans. Keeping his spirit and his songs alive is something I hold very close to my heart.”

Jamie Cerreta, president of U.S. and Canada at Peermusic, said, “Gram’s music is an enduring testament to how great songs remain in our hearts. All of us at Peermusic are so honored to represent his songs and to see his work celebrated through his recent induction into the Rock ‘n’ Roll Hall of Fame. I am personally so happy to be working with Polly and Vector Management to help another generation discover the greateness of Gram Parsons.” —  Ariel King

Electric Feel Publishing EU has signed James Bell, better known as Yami. The songwriter and vocalist began working in the industry alongside Brian Eno and has worked with artists including RAYE and Roots Manuva, and he also co-wrote Tiësto’s hit song, “The Business.”

“Everyone I knew on EF were always the coolest and most talented people, now I get to be part of that and that’s a real privilege,” Bell said in a statement. “I know that with their dedicated team and my ability to span across genres, we will do great things.”

Austin Rosen, Electric Feel Entertainment’s CEO and founder, said in a statement, “What stands out to me about Yami is his ability to create music that connects across so many different artists and sounds. From the work he’s already done to the projects he has coming up, he has a real instinct for finding something special in every collaboration. We’re excited to be working with him and to help bring his vision to life as he continues to grow.”

Sureeta Nayyar, head of A&R, U.K., at Electric Feel added, “We’re incredibly excited to welcome Yami to Electric Feel. His ability to work across a diverse range of artists and genres speaks to his versatility as a songwriter and his instinct for creating records that resonate. With an exciting slate of upcoming releases and development projects in the works, there’s so much potential ahead. We’re looking forward to supporting his growth, championing his creativity and helping bring his vision to life.” — Ariel King

Peermusic has signed a worldwide publishing deal with Latin Grammy nominated artist Isadora. The Miami-based artist of Puerto Rican, Venezuelan, and Italian descent laces Caribbean rhythms with pop and tropical music, resulting in songs such as “La Bici” and “Agüita con Sal.”

“She is not only an incredible performer with a powerful voice and a distinct artistic identity, but also an exceptionally talented and versatile songwriter,” Elizabeth Rodda, President, US Latin, Latin America and Global Society Relations, said in a statement. “Her ability to move effortlessly between performing and creating in the studio, while maintaining her unique voice and charisma, is what makes her so special. We are thrilled to welcome her to peermusic, where she joins an extraordinary roster of women songwriters who continue to push creative boundaries and shape the future of music.”

In 2025, the rising singer-songwriter—who’s a University of Miami’s Frost School of Music alum—was nominated for best new artist at the Latin Grammys, and she dropped her debut studio album La Isla, a 13-song set that celebrates her Island heritage. “Songwriting has always been one of the most important parts of my journey as an artist and one of my greatest passions, so finding a home that truly believes in my voice, my message, and my vision means so much to me,” she shared. “Joining the peermusic family is especially meaningful because of the history we share and the support they’ve shown me since the very beginning. It’s a full-circle moment.” — Jessica Roiz

Position Music has signed Masego to a worldwide publishing deal. The Jamaican-American artist-songwriter-musician released Fix Your Face, his third studio album, in July. His 2017 breakthrough single “Tadow” featuring FKJ has since been certified platinum. Masego (born Micah Davis) earned his first Grammy nomination for the 2021 deluxe EP Studying Abroad: Extended Stay.

“Masego is a generational creative talent and a true artist in every sense of the word,” commented Position Music vp of A&R Delmar Powell. “His ability to seamlessly blend jazz, R&B, hip-hop and global influences has created a sound that’s uniquely his own, while continuing to push the boundaries of Black music. Beyond his incredible gifts as a songwriter, producer and musician, I genuinely believe there are few artists who can match what he brings to the stage. His live performances are second to none. Masego represents the kind of artistry that transcends trends and leaves a lasting cultural impact.” — Gail Mitchell

#648. JO1’s ‘IGNITE’ Tops Japan Hot 100 as Hiromi Ohta’s 1975 Hit ‘Momen no Handkerchief’ Debuts

Plus: BUDDiiS' "Mugendai LOVE!!!" jumps 48-2.

JO1‘s “IGNITE” soars to No. 1 on the Billboard Japan Hot 100 chart released Nov. 25.

The title track of the group’s 11th single “AAO,” released Nov. 18, serves as the opener for the TV anime Tokyo Revengers War of the Three Titans Arc. The song launched with 678,171 copies to lead sales while placing high across other metrics, including No. 2 for downloads and No. 6 for radio airplay. The song’s total points grew about 7.7-fold from the previous week.

BUDDiiS’ “Mugendai LOVE!!!” jumps 48-2. Also released Nov. 18, the track sold 251,610 copies to place at No. 2 for sales, with total points up about 6.2-fold week over week. EBiDAN’s “Yes! Tokyo” comes in at No. 3, leading video views and placing at No. 2 for streaming. Ayumu Imazu’s “Musubi” holds steady at No. 4, topping streaming and placing at No. 9 for downloads. FRUITS ZIPPER’s “Power of Love” surges 64-16. The track comes in at No. 4 for sales (37,289 copies), and total points grew 155.1% week over week. Lienel’s “Ai no Dabada” climbs 61-29 with No. 8 for sales (12,882 copies) and total points up 64.7%.

Fujii Kaze, who held his Fujii Kaze Piano Recital on Nov. 20 and 21 and streamed it on YouTube, saw “Garden” climb 94-80 and “Hana” return to the chart for the first time in about a year. Hiromi Ohta’s “Momen no Handkerchief,” a vintage hit from 1975, debuts at No. 93. The Billboard Japan Hot 100 combines physical and digital sales, audio streams, radio airplay, video views and karaoke data.

#647. Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

When humans live on the moon, we'll need to grow food on the moon, too.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon.

To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal.

"We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement. "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon."

To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith, the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions.

The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement.

The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth.
