#609. Awkwafina ‘Really Goes for It’ in Surrealist Cancer Drama ‘Kate Might Die,’ Says Director Mercedes Bryce Morgan

Director Mercedes Bryce Morgan is adamant: the world isn’t ready for Awkwafina’s performance in “Kate Might Die”.

“It’s quite incredible to see. She gives it her all and really goes for it,” she says.

“We’ve already seen her in ‘The Farewell’ [which won her a Golden Globe] and we’ve seen her do comedy. On top of that, she brings such likeability and vulnerability to her roles. To me, there was no point in making this movie unless we had the perfect person.” Related Stories Jeff Goldblum Breaks Into 'Wicked' Song While Reflecting on His 'Unexpectedly Enduring Career' at Marrakech: 'You Just Follow Your Curiosity and Your Heart' Salma Hayek Pinault and Saúl ‘Canelo’ Álvarez Board Cannes Short Film Palme d’Or Winner ‘For the Opponents,’ Igniting Its Oscar Campaign (EXCLUSIVE)

In “Kate Might Die,” Awkwafina plays Kate McAnneny, a young woman diagnosed with breast cancer. Suddenly, she has to juggle her career, family, treatment and her husband’s sobriety while figuring out what she wants for her future. If she has one.

Produced by Whitewater Films and co-produced by Balcony 9 and Sweetheart Entertainment, it won four awards at the U.S. in Progress co-production forum at TAURON American Film Festival in Poland. You can find the full list of awards here:

Anthony Ramos, Ken Jeong, Zosia Mamet, Jimmi Simpson, Lauren Tom and Ben Wang also star.

“Kate Might Die” is actually inspired by a true story.

“Kate McAnneny is a real person,” says Morgan.

“She’s a production designer who was diagnosed with breast cancer when she was training for the New York Marathon. What was so wonderful was taking this real human experience and amplifying it. We just took that whole playground and ran with it.”

McAnneny was on set when they were filming.

“She really trusted us, and that made this movie possible. We got to see her develop relationships with the actors because she saw her family members in them. There’s even a cameo of her in the movie: when Awkwafina sees the real Kate, they look back at each other. Only people who know them will notice it.”

Despite the diagnosis that shakes up Kate’s life, it’s not your usual cancer drama.

“I was wondering: What is it like to experience something like that? It just becomes surreal. In the film, there are scenes where Awkwafina is being chased by her boobs, or there are 100 animated versions of her,” laughs Morgan.

“We’re used to seeing cancer movies where people get that phone call or their doctor tells them the news. Here, she’s on the subway when everything becomes so loud. She can’t hear her doctor telling her she has cancer, but there’s an a cappella group singing and telling her that she’s going to die, incorporating her name in the song.”

She adds: “That’s just one example of how our movie takes a different, more surreal path than maybe another one with the same storyline would.”

Bringing (dark) comedy into the story was a no-brainer.

“Whenever traumatic or catastrophic things happen in life, you need a moment of levity. You kind of need that hope. My favorite movies – and the kind of movies I like to create – explore the full range of human emotions. When I go to the cinema, I want to experience something intense and shocking. I was looking at combining all of those things.”

Her actors were game to try that as well.

“Ken Jeong and Awkwafina are making each other laugh, but they’re also making each other cry. As long as it’s emotionally true, it doesn’t matter what genre your film is or how much you base it in reality. Ultimately, that’s what shines through to people.”

#608. An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.

#607. Jeff Goldblum Breaks Into ‘Wicked’ Song While Reflecting on His ‘Unexpectedly Enduring Career’ at Marrakech: ‘You Just Follow Your Curiosity and Your Heart’

Jeff Goldblum showed off his vocal chops Wednesday during a wide-ranging conversation about his almost 60-year cinema career at the Marrakech Film Festival.

During the on-stage talk, the actor launched into a tune from the soundtrack of “Wicked” — in which he plays the Wizard — crooning for the audience, “I’m a sentimental man who always longed to be a father.”

This wasn’t the first musical performance Goldblum had delivered during the Moroccan fest. Related Stories The Ultimate Advent Calendar for Jet-Setters: Artist Laila Gohar's Chocolate-Filled Creation Is Inspired by 24 Luxury Destinations Hollywood Gets Roasted in Satirical Picture Book ‘We Make a Movie’: ‘I Loved Your Script … Now Change Everything’ (EXCLUSIVE)

On Saturday, Goldblum received an honorary Étoile d’Or at a glitzy ceremony, where the actor was introduced by Tilda Swinton, who praised her “Grand Budapest Hotel” and “Asteroid City” co-star as a “unicorn” and an “incomparable presence in cinema.”

After a tribute video showcased his iconic roles across nearly six decades on screen, the curtain rose to reveal Goldblum — an accomplished pianist and jazz musician to boot — seated behind a grand piano, from which he serenaded a rapt crowd.

During Wednesday’s conversation, Goldblum shared anecdotes about his many collaborators, crediting an ethos of “conscientiously and daily and routinely exploring” for his remarkable longevity and insisting: “You just follow your curiosity and your heart.”

Over the course of the rollicking and wide-ranging chat, the actor looked back at his storied career, from his first role as “Freak No. 1” in Charles Bronson’s “Death Wish” to his “lively, robust and delicious collaboration” with David Cronenberg on “The Fly” and his partnership with the “masterful” Steven Spielberg on “Jurassic Park.”

With some 150 film credits to his name, Goldblum reflected on the range of roles he’s performed over the years, insisting that his “unexpectedly enduring career has been luck as much as anything else” while stressing the importance of remaining open-minded about whatever work comes his way.

“I’ve tried to stay open. And especially navigating this world of professional opportunities, where you’re just lucky to keep going, and not being particularly strategic about what pool shot will lead to what outcome. But just going, ‘Jeez, what interests me now and what might be really exciting and educational to do?’” he said.

“I think that all this so-called work I’ve done has made me in some ways what I am,” he continued. “I’ve been lucky that I’ve had a so-called career that cumulatively has added up to a body of something, and a continuation of something. And yes, I’ve had the work itself.”

A voluble presence on stage, Goldblum recalled his early acting education in New York, where he studied under the legendary William Esper alongside Larry David. (“He’s never asked me to be on ‘Curb Your Enthusiasm.’ Isn’t that horrible?” the actor deadpanned.) He also lavished praise on Daniel Day-Lewis, “who so eloquently and inspiringly and nobly” embodies the life of an actor, even while Goldblum himself downplayed a life in moviemaking as “the serious business of play.”

“I’ve been a lucky guy. I’m a lucky guy to have met these people and worked with these people,” he said.

As well as the tribute award, the festival is screening four films from the actor’s oeuvre, featuring his beloved and iconic performances in Lawrence Kasdan’s ’80s ensemble comedy-drama “The Big Chill,” David Cronenberg’s classic body horror “The Fly,” Roland Emmerich’s alien-invasion blockbuster “Independence Day” and “Jurassic Park,” the first installment in the dinosaur franchise juggernaut.

Goldblum appears to be making the most of his first visit to Morocco, hamming it up on the red carpet ahead of the opening ceremony on Nov. 20 and sitting front and center on Tuesday as “Paper Tiger” director James Gray delivered his own reminiscences to the audience in Marrakech.

On Wednesday, the actor basked in the standing ovation he received ahead of his conversation. Later he invited the audience into a parlor game where a participant names a movie, and the next player picks an actor from the same film, creating a six-degrees-of-separation effect linking together directors and stars across the generations.

Hearing the title “I Heart Huckabees” from the audience, Goldblum namechecked director David O. Russell, whose latest film, “Madden,” stars Nicolas Cage as the Hall of Fame football coach and legendary TV commentator and Christian Bale as late Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis.

“Christian Bale takes us to ‘Empire of the Sun’ takes us to Steven Spielberg takes us to ‘Jurassic Park’ takes us to Jeff Goldblum,” the actor said. As the audience applauded, he added: “That’s our show. Drive safely.”

The Marrakech Film Festival runs through Nov. 28.

#606. Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

Building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.

The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.

To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.

Unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders

Previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.

The University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.

"There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum said.

The team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.

However, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.

"These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum said. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet."

Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases

Before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several important questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.

Despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery

For McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.

"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum said.

McCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.

Although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.

"It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he said. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early."

"We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper.

New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.

NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity.

As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf, the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived "red giant" phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris.

During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space.

To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming.

"Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action."

The team was able to determine that this gas shell of IRAS 06530-0213 is around half a light-year wide and was ejected into space around 6,500 years ago. It represents the first direct evidence of the last thermal pulse before this kind of star enters the final phase of its life.

The team thinks that for around 2,000 years after the pulse, the star lost mass at a lower rate. This mass loss then increased sharply over the following 1,000 years. This led to the creation of a lumpy shell of gas now seen as a tangle of material filaments around the dying star. The fact that these filaments have a spiral shape could indicate that IRAS 06530-0213 has an unseen partner orbiting it, stirring the gas.

Meanwhile, the hourglass-shaped nebula immediately around the star began to take shape around 700 years ago, meaning that the red giant phase for IRAS 06530-0213 only ended very recently, in cosmic terms at least.

There are also unexpected elements to the ALMA observations of IRAS 06530-0213.

The team discovered an unexpected abundance of heavy versions, or isotopes, of elements like carbon, oxygen and nitrogen around IRAS 06530-0213.

This doesn't conform to models of how stars like IRAS 06530-0213 forge elements and mix them into their surroundings, though similar signatures have been seen around odd stellar objects, with violent bursts of nuclear fusion thought to be the cause.As well as seeing something unexpected, the researchers didn't detect something they expected to observe.

Dying stars like IRAS 06530-0213 have previously been known to have companions, typically sitting with them inside compact disks of dust. These disks are indirect evidence of material being dragged from the close companion star to the dying star. This is a process scientists have used to explain jet-sculpted hourglass shapes.

However, ALMA failed to detect such disk around IRAS 06530. The team suggests that this could be because a disk existed, albeit briefly, during which time it powered a short burst of high-speed jets that helped sculpt the hourglass, following this the disk simply faded away.

"Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres," Sahai concluded. "IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we've been using."The team's research was published on Friday (Nov. 20) in The Astrophysical Journal.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

'Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner.''

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#602. How ‘Backrooms’ Artisans Transformed YouTube Series Into Cinema’s Favorite Liminal Space Using 30,000 Square Feet of Sets and Four Sound Stages

Before Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” became a $400 million global box office success, it was a YouTube series with 22 episodes, each ranging from two minutes to 45 minutes exploring the “Backrooms” lore.

The series was a viral hit, and so was the movie. However, for the film’s production designer Danny Vermette and visual effects supervisor Ed Douglas, neither was initially aware of the series. After receiving a call from the film’s producer, Chris Ferguson, both Douglas and Vermette went down the rabbit hole and dove right in. Related Stories Box Office: 'Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping' Targets Huge Debut Above $100 Million Thanksgiving Box Office: 'Focker In-Law' and Disney's 'Hexed' Vie for No. 2 Behind 'Sunrise on the Reaping'

Speaking with Variety, Douglas, whose work is shortlisted for Oscar consideration, recalled his first response: “Is this real? Is this CG? What is this going to be?” After jumping on a call with Parsons, he learned about how the world had been built using Blender, 3D creation software used for modeling, animation, CGI, rendering, visual effects and simulation.” He says, “We started talking about what our process would be. Would this be a very traditional, film VFX process or would we bring in a hybrid process with the Kane Parsons Blender workflow? It was that combined process that we built.”

Set in 1991, the film stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a furniture emporium owner who discovers a portal in the basement of his store. Clark becomes obsessed with this alternate world, a never-ending series of liminal spaces lined with carpet and yellow wallpaper. Vermette spoke with friends who were familiar with “Backrooms” and Parsons. “I fast realized how versed Kane was in this universe, and how truly immersed he had been for several years and realized I needed to catch up with some of this lore and the theory behind how it works if we were to figure out a way to make this work and build this universe together.”

Collectively, the team decided the set would be a practical build to enable the actors to be fully immersed in the world. To truly pull it off, there would need to be a handoff to VFX, thus combining practical builds and visual effects to bring “Backrooms” to life. Vermette explained, “I had the constraints of budget and square footage. So it was about putting a square peg in a square hole. I knew exactly what our limitations were. The more we’re grounded in the reality, the more the visual effects will work, will sell. Let’s take the practical world as far as we can, and then extend and enhance.”

He adds, “If the actors are in the space interacting with it, let’s build it for real. And then building all those sets for real gave us a model so we could make sure we’re mimicking exactly how the wallpaper works, how the ceilings work, how the light works. And then when we get into the clipping, people passing through the walls.”

Clark’s furniture store basement was right next to the first backroom space. The actors could walk from one to the other, and the camera could pass through one right to the other. Douglas points out, “We put blue screens up on either side as we were filming these, and then in VFX post-production, we would add the walls back in.”

In the final movie, what sells it is that you have this shadow intersecting in this very unreal way. Says Douglas, “The visual language of this wasn’t like a fantasy movie. There’s no sparkles, distortion or ripples. It was two computerized objects sliding straight through each other, so there’s nowhere to hide. It was very challenging, very meticulous work.”

Much of the effort was focused on creating vertical liminal spacing in the film. For the Vertigo Room, which Mary (Renate Reinsve) discovers while fleeing from Pirate Clark, Parsons says it was a straightforward build. They had found a building in Downtown Vancouver, owned by a bank. “We hollowed out a skyscraper.”

But it was really helped with the use of blue screen. “We built everything the actor is interacting with physically. As Mary walks along the pathway, the hallway that she’s going through before is a separate set, with a separate door and then we’re jumping over into an L shape. We’ve got a ceiling that goes far out enough that the staircase with the little trap door those are real tiles that she’s going up into — and there is enough of a return when she goes through the door and climbs out, so she can safely hoist herself up a bit.”

In the end, “Backrooms” came together with a set that measured over 30,000 square feet and used four stages.

#601. CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

It also creates new opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics

The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

When particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale."

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth."

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

"We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons."

The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

This name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

For now, the new measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

"There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.

"The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data."

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

Researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to important advances in understanding nature.

"This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success."

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful new way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

#600. ‘Focker In-Law’ Director on Casting Ariana Grande, Why Barbra Streisand and Dustin Hoffman Didn’t Return and What the Ending Means for Another Sequel

Over the years, “Meet the Parents” writer John Hamburg would exchange the occasional text or email with his collaborators from the 2000 movie to ask whether anyone had another sequel idea. (They had already revisited the characters, mismatched in-laws portrayed by Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, to outsized commercial success in 2004’s “Meet the Fockers” and 2010’s “Little Fockers.”) But nothing else stuck — until they realized Stiller was the same age as De Niro’s character in the first film, a comedy about male nurse Gaylord “Greg” Focker who goes through hijinks hell when he’s introduced to his girlfriend’s family, including her intimidating father Jack Byrnes. Related Stories Generative AI Indian Feature 'Maharaja in Denims,' Inspired by Sikh Ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Sets April 2027 Release (EXCLUSIVE) Cole Sprouse Says He Didn't Make 'Substantial Money' on 'Riverdale' Until Season 4: TV Is 'Not as Profitable for Actors Anymore'

“It felt like a way back into the story,” says Hamburg, best known for “Zoolander” and “I Love You, Man,” in addition to the “Focker” films. “Greg Focker finds himself where Jack was all those years ago. What a full-circle moment.”

The result is “Focker In-Law,” a battle of wits that plays out as Greg’s son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) brings home his new girlfriend, a former FBI hostage negotiator named Olivia (Ariana Grande). The new installment, written and directed by Hamburg, takes place as the entire family — including Greg and Jack’s wives Pam and Dina (Teri Polo and Blythe Danner), as well as Greg and Pam’s daughter Samantha (Beanie Feldstein) and her boyfriend Eduardo (Eduardo Franco) — return to Long Island to celebrate Jack’s 80th birthday.

Ahead of the big-screen release — “Focker In-Law” opens in theaters on Nov. 25 — Hamburg spoke to Variety about reconnecting with Stiller and De Niro, Grande’s comedic chops and why Barbra Streisand and Dustin Hoffman didn’t return as Greg’s parents.

It was surreal. The first time I was at the Byrnes family home in Oyster Bay, Long Island, I was 29, and now I’m coming back in my 50s. That was my first big job in the business.

From time to time, the original group who made the first few movies would text or email to say, “Is there any idea?” But it wasn’t something on my mind. Peter Cramer at Universal was a big proponent of this movie, and he jump-started it, saying, “We would be interested if you guys would be interested.” We were all driven by one thing: “Do we have a story that we’re excited to tell?” It wasn’t “let’s cash in,” I promise. We all were happy doing other things.

It was really joyful to be back with those guys. Their chemistry is incredible. The fact that we have this history helps on set. There’s so much trust.

We knew we needed to bring a big new element to this, just like we had in “Meet the Fockers,” bringing in Dustin Hoffman and Barbra Streisand as Greg’s parents. Ariana was the perfect person. She’s hilarious, and she’s got great timing. I can’t believe she’s been in as few big movies as she has, because she’s so skilled. Bringing her in was this injection of awesomeness. She would light up the set. I really love her energy, and she’s so much fun to be around and to work with — so engaged and committed and professional and early. She was always the first one there.

Oh, they were totally game. Ben Stiller is basically the most committed actor who could ever exist. As long as he thinks it’s right for the story, he will go for it, 100%. The first day of rehearsal — Ben and Ari had met, but they hadn’t rehearsed — was the Heimlich maneuver scene. So it was literally, like, “Ben, Ari — say hi to each other. OK, now you’re gonna get behind Ben and start giving him the Heimlich.” Ari was tentative at first because they didn’t know each other well. And Ben’s like, “Go for it. Don’t worry.” There were no stunt doubles.

That was a very physical scene. That was crazy to shoot. Ari took the kitchen stuff really seriously and took multiple lessons with a world-class chef to learn knife skills. It was the sous chef of my good friend Dan Barber, who owns Blue Hill at Stone Barns. And then the flame, it wasn’t done all with CGI. There was a special-effects flame that shot up in Ben’s face, and then Ariana was swatting him, and he was pushing back. They were both so in it. Ben was saying, “Swat me in the face,” and Ariana was saying, “Put your hand on my face to push me away!” There was no being shy around each other.

De Niro, at 82 years old, was cruising on that bike. He has this very unique way of riding a bike. His shoulders kind of rock back and forth, and he was super into it. Ariana took lessons to get as proficient as possible on the bike. Ben is a big cyclist, so he slipped into that pretty easily.

Bob is a fitness guy. He takes it really seriously. I was talking to his trainer and he was like, “No, Bob hits it hard many days of the week.” But Jack Byrnes is suddenly into wellness in a way he hadn’t been in the previous movies, so Bob got even more ripped and stronger for the role. He went full Jake LaMotta in “Raging Bull.” Bob and Ben knew there was a scene where they were both going to be in speedos, so they’re like, “We gotta go for it.”

You’d have to ask Bob. I’m not sure, but Bob has kids and grandkids. He’s around young people all the time, so Bob’s pretty hip. I think he knew. He might not let that on, but he’d be like, “I know, John. I know.”

Look, I have no one to blame but myself. I wrote that line. Maybe there’s more to mine, but only if it’s organic and feels like there’s a reason for it to exist. Talk to me after Thanksgiving weekend.

I have some people in mind, but there’s no way I could talk about this right now.

I was a fan of Cole’s, and flight attendants are very important in these movies. Rachel Tenner, our casting director, was like, “What about Cole Escola?” Immediately, my producers and I were like, “That would be perfect.” Cole might be one of the funniest human beings I’ve ever been around, and they made Ben and Ariana die laughing for those three days that they were on set.

I wanted to bring back the lie detector, because that’s such an important part of the franchise. And now we have Olivia Jones, who is FBI, so she might know her way around a lie detector. You’re probably going to have a dinner table scene. The dinner table scene in the first movie ends in such a funny way, with Greg breaking the urn of Jack’s mom and Jinx [the cat] peeing on the ashes. I don’t know that we’re ever going to top that, but what can we do that will take the audience by surprise and feel right for the story? So I wrote the part with Greg baby-birding Grandpa Jack. It’s a pretty epic moment. My fellow filmmakers on this movie were a little skeptical, and I’m wrong about a lot of stuff, but I was like, “Guys, I feel it in my gut. This is gonna work.”

That’s really important, because it’s been a long time since “Meet the Parents.” I have to assume that many people aren’t that familiar, or maybe they saw it a long time ago. I wanted to make this movie work if you’d never seen any of the “Meet the Parents,” as a funny, heartfelt, character-based comedy. But then, of course, it is a “Meet the Parents” movie, so there’s going to be certain touchstones. My job was finding fresh ways in.

Yes, of course. They were so incredible in “Meet the Fockers.” But I wanted to bring it back to the simplicity of the original “Meet the Parents.” Dustin and Barbra are so iconic that I didn’t want to bring them back in a smaller part if I couldn’t service their characters, because I had all these new characters. If I brought them back, I would have to take away from Olivia, Henry, Samantha and Eduardo. It was a hard choice. Not that they would have agreed to come back. But for this story, it didn’t feel like the movie could hold all of that. But maybe in a fifth one…

It’s got to be the writing. No, I’m just kidding. If you use that quote, you have to say I was joking. I believe it’s because the themes are relatable and timeless. Everybody, at one point in their lives, is probably going to introduce their significant other to their families.

As far as making the movie, it wasn’t that different. Universal gave us so much support. One thing is studios literally stopped making this type of comedy for theaters. It’s hard to point to the last one. I’m not talking about hilarious movies like the “Naked Gun” or “Scary Movie” reboots. Those are a little different, because they’re in their own sub-genre. But the movies I made or watched in the ’90s and 2000s stopped getting made. They moved to streaming, which can be great, but it’s just different. I think people were missing that communal feeling of being in a theater with hundreds of people and sharing laughter at cringe moments.

#599. Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."

#598. A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

For more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, new research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

In a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

"The claim that mutation is slower for important genes is a triumph of hype over substance," said Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the new paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely."

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution

The conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

However, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

At first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

The problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations

Another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Important genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are quickly eliminated from populations.

Professor Hurst said: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more important genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'."

This distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory

To investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

The scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

Dr. Radrizzani said: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date."

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more important for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

They assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

If the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

Professor Hurst said: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate."

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

The team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more important genes receive special protection.

Dr. Radrizzani said: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate."

That does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

Professor Hurst said: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm."

The research therefore provides new support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most important genes by reducing how often they mutate.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds."

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

#596. ‘Gugu’s World’ Team on the Diversity of Brazilian Cinema and Championing Films That ‘Respect the Storyteller’

The creative team behind the coming-of-age drama celebrates a long journey that has culminated in making a star out of newcomer Yuri Gomes and connecting with audiences across Brazil and the world

In the nine months since “Gugu’s World” premiered in Berlin, director Allan Deberton has had only the most “joyful experiences.” By the time the filmmaker sits down with Variety to discuss the whirlwind, the film has just opened in its home country of Brazil, turning its young star into a phenomenon.

That star is Yuri Gomes, who plays the titular Gugu. The boy is the epitome of freedom, zigzagging across a dirt field with a football, then breaking into a dance sequence the moment he hears the throbbing beats of Brazilian brega music. Yes, those around him judge him, including stern dad Batista (Lázaro Ramos), but Gugu is sheltered by the love of grandmother Dilma (Teca Pereira). The two live together in a small town in Ceará, their loving home and safe cocoon until the day Dilma’s health deteriorates due to a rapidly developing case of Alzheimer’s. Related Stories Michael Urie to Host 79th Writers Guild Awards in New York (EXCLUSIVE) MasterClass Courses -- From Spike Lee, Mark Cuban and Martha Stewart -- Are 50% Off This Black Friday

“Gugu’s World” follows Deberton’s “Pacarrete” and reunites the director with screenwriter André Araújo, who originated the story. The tale of this energetic boy resonated deeply with the filmmaker, who knew he needed a “great cast” to do justice to the “responsibility” of tackling the issues in the script, from talking about young queerness to dealing with caring responsibilities and progressive disorders. Deberton landed two of Brazil’s great screen stars in Ramos and Pereira, but the process of finding Gugu was a much more complex, lengthy operation. The film team saw over 700 kids and eventually found Gomes, a star-in-the-making.

“We needed an actor who had the spirit of Gugu,” says producer Karen Castanho of Biônica Filmes. “But today, the great challenge of filming kids is that, because of social media, kids are not very spontaneous. Yuri is the opposite of that.”

Deberton worked closely with casting director and AD Luciana Vieira to ensure that not only Gomes but the wider cast of children were “very natural.” “We simply see children being children. We don’t see kids acting. I think that’s very strong in the film.”

The director said it is “transformative” to work with children. He enjoyed the experience so much that he decided to replicate it for his next project, “Adoption,” dealing with his personal experience adopting his son. “What they put on the screen is very truthful. We need to be open to that gaze, which is pure, intimate, truthful and that makes us feel alive.”

The film presented a great challenge to Ramos, an actor-director with decades of experience and one of the most recognizable names in Brazil thanks to his work on telenovelas and films such as “Madame Satã” and “Carandiru.” Ramos is more widely known for his loving, well-humored roles, so playing a stern father dealing with internalized homophobia and unable to accept his son was difficult.

“My first read of [Batista] was one that is very distant from the dad I aim to be,” he said. “I was looking to villainize that figure, to signal his flaws, like an alert call. But when we started rehearsing, he gained richness and a much more interesting personality, which is this man who does care about his child, who seeks to be closer to his child, but he doesn’t have the resources.”

Asked about the physicality of his character, who is often contained in contrast to Gugu’s penchant for movement, Ramos shared the complex process. During rehearsals, it felt “curious” to Ramos how he couldn’t mimic Gomes’ movements. The two often danced together or moved together between takes, but Ramos returned to introspection when cameras rolled. “It was good to encounter that vitality of his to understand the opposition we’d aim for in each scene,” he said.

Pereira, on the other hand, was able to imbue Dilma with a lot of herself, such as “her joy for life, that animated way of living and the way she cares for her grandson,” she noted. The role was still quite different from everything she had done previously, with the experience made even more special thanks to the relationship she developed with Gomes. “Luciana Vieira gave us exercises for us to develop that care, to develop a bond,” she recalled. “It was great. Yuri is an intelligent, clever child, as well as talented.”

Working on an indie project always brings a set of challenges, but shooting with a large ensemble cast mostly of children and setting the production in Quixadá, a small city in the inland of Ceará, added massively to Castanho’s plate.

Despite the city being a frequent production hub, the film team wanted to avoid “obvious locations,” turning the city into a base camp. “Most of the locations were within one hour of the city, with a big team, to sets without any infrastructure. We had to literally bring everything to film in these places, which involved traveling one hour every day.”

“At the same time, we needed a city that could host all these people,” added the producer. “The logistical challenge was huge. The background actors are all from the region, but the team is very diverse. Brazil is a country of continental dimensions; we had professionals from all over Brazil. The greatest challenge for us was logistical.”

Deberton noted that the local population completely embraced the project, and the film team worked closely with all background extras to ensure they were comfortable with the costume and production design and felt integrated into the production. Ramos said he “loves shooting on location” and ended up staying longer in Quixadá than he was originally supposed to. “I live in an urban center, I’m very agitated, very rushed,” he said. “And there’s a timing there of the effect of a smaller city, where people know each other, where people have time to chat and I think that ended up influencing me too.”

When asked what “Gugu’s World” communicates about Brazil to international audiences and what they want the film to be in dialogue with when it meets audiences all over the world, the team Castanho is quick to say she wants people to understand the diversity of Brazilian cinema. “This is a small film with a big heart and, especially in this moment in the world, I think we all need that love.”

Deberton echoes that thought, saying he often felt that Brazilian films were “put in a box” as a type of cinema that would connect with cinephiles but not broad audiences. “I think it’s the opposite: when we have access to powerful stories, to characters that transform, that connection happens naturally and genuinely with the audience,” he said.

“This progress that we’re seeing with national cinema shows a quality of directors, of teams and producers,” added Pereira, noting the great momentum of her national cinema, with standout international hits such as “I’m Still Here” and “The Secret Agent” projecting Brazilian films to the world.

“As Allan says, regionality is very important because we don’t want to stay just in the big urban centers,” added the actress. “The quality of the work depends also on the opportunities. Brazil is very diverse. We have a lot to show still, and a lot to do still … And for me it’s very important. I want and hope that all this results in more jobs for many people, because we need to talk about ourselves. And that should be seen by the whole world.”

Ramos wrapped the conversation by humorously stating he would bring a “contentious” subject to the table, which is the need for the regulation of streamers in Brazil so that independent productions can benefit from the market they have helped build, as well as revising how partnerships with major studios and production companies are forged.

“After the pandemic, we went through a period in which, due to market needs, we made some concessions and negotiations, and made many films without identity,” he said. “People watched a film and wouldn’t even know the name of the protagonist at the end of the movie. Or they would be faced with a storytelling model based on either an algorithm or on the desires of another country.”

“Gugu’s World” goes against the grain in this sense, according to the veteran performer. “This film struggled to find partners and financiers for a long time,” he went on. “So let’s take the opportunity to get people to consider the current state of filmmaking, watch this film and go back to respecting the storyteller, which I think is an important message, because otherwise we get a lot of tepid or similar movies.”

Ahead of the announcement, organizers behind the parade had been monitoring the weather situation all week, worrying that strong winds in New York City would ground the iconic balloons. Over 100 balloons and balloon handlers were set to be on display in celebration of the parade’s 100th anniversary. Buckaroo Bob the Minion, Joe Cool, Mickey’s Sorcerer’s Apprentice and Billie Brightpaw were among the balloon characters that had to be grounded.

Preparations for the parade balloons take months, with a village of creatives working behind the scenes to bring everything together. As early as July, the parade’s concept artist begins working on both balloon and float designs. By September, the parade’s costume designer, Kimberly Montgomery, starts piecing together over 5,000 costumes and collaborating with partners to ensure she has the right colors for the balloon handlers and accurate designs.

Float performances on the schedule include Natasha Bedingfield, McKenna Grace, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Queen Latifah and a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty.

“Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade brings the extraordinary together: iconic entertainers and emerging talent, artistry and imagination, hometown pride, cherished traditions and the thrill of discovering something new,” said Sharon Otterman, Macy’s chief marketing officer. “For our 100th Parade, we’re creating a celebration of unprecedented scale and will deliver an unforgettable Thanksgiving for millions across the country.”

NBC and Peacock are still set to air “Countdown to Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade” Wednesday at 8 p.m. ET.

SpaceX launched another classified mission for the U.S. Space Force (USSF) today (Nov. 24), sending an unknown payload toward orbit from California.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base's Space Launch Complex-4E at TK11:08 a.m. ET (1508 GMT), carrying the U.S. Space Force's USSF-266 mission. It was the fourth mission SpaceX has launched for the military branch this month.

While details about the mission's payload weren't disclosed, it's the fifth space launch in support of U.S. national security in the last two weeks, and comes amid efforts by the Space Force to expand its communications and tracking capabilities.

About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Falcon 9's first-stage booster separated from the rocket's upper stage, which continued toward low Earth orbit with the classified payload. The booster, meanwhile, began a descent toward SpaceX's Of Course I Still Love You droneship in the Pacific Ocean, where it touched down approximately eight and a half minutes after launch.

Tuesday's launch marked the 29th flight for this Falcon 9 booster, B1081, which previously launched NASA's Crew-7 astronaut mission to the International Space Station, the PACE and EarthCARE science satellites, two other classified Space Force launches (USSF-153 and USSF-481), and 16 Starlink missions.

Previous classified Space Force launches have fueled speculation about the possible deployment of SpaceX's Starshield satellites, which are designed for national security applications. Starshield is an adapted spacecraft design developed from SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation that supports military operations with capabilities like Earth observation and secure communications. SpaceX has not confirmed whether USSF-266 is carrying Starshield spacecraft.

USSF-266 follows three other classified Space Force missions launched by SpaceX from Vandenberg earlier this month: USSF-432 on Nov. 6, USSF-627 on Nov. 11 and USSF-317 on Nov. 20, as well as a National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) launch, NROL-136, on Nov. 22. Those missions were also launched aboard Falcon 9 rockets, also with undisclosed payloads.
